title: Five major features hidden behind an unlabeled overflow menu
description: Five primary features (فهرس الأجزاء/Juz index, خطة الختمة/Khatmah plan, الملاحظات/Notes, المراجعة والحفظ/Memorization, الفهرس الموضوعي/Thematic index) are reachable ONLY via a 3-dot PopupMenuButton on the Home AppBar. There is no bottom-nav entry, no card, and no on-screen affordance for any of them. The icon is the generic Icons.more_vert with no tooltip and no label.
impact: Core app capabilities (Juz browsing, Khatmah scheduling, note-taking, memorization, thematic search) are effectively undiscoverable. Many users will never find them, since a kebab menu reads as 'minor settings' rather than 'half the app's features'. The features also vanish entirely if the user is on the Bookmarks or Settings tab.
recommendation: Surface these as a visible grid/row of quick-action cards on the Home body, or move them into a richer bottom-nav / drawer with labels and icons. At minimum add a tooltip to the PopupMenuButton (e.g. 'المزيد') and give each item a leading icon.
evidence: PopupMenuButton<String>(icon: const Icon(Icons.more_vert), ... itemBuilder: (context) => const [ PopupMenuItem(value: 'juz', child: Text('فهرس الأجزاء')), ... ]

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual code. home_screen.dart lines 88-99 contain exactly the cited PopupMenuButton(icon: Icons.more_vert) with no `tooltip` argument and five PopupMenuItems (juz/khatmah/notes/memorization/thematic) that have plain Text children and no leading icons. I confirmed these are the ONLY entry points to those five features: app_router.dart defines all five as routes on the ROOT navigator (parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey, lines 67-102), so they render full-screen with no bottom nav; app_shell.dart's NavigationBar exposes only 3 destinations (home/bookmarks/settings, lines 46-62); and an exhaustive grep for the route name literals/RouteNames across lib/ found no quick-action cards, drawer, or any other pushNamed/goNamed calls — only the router definitions and this one menu. So the discoverability claim is factually accurate: five substantial features (Juz index, Khatmah completion plan, Notes, Memorization/review, Thematic index) are reachable solely through an unlabeled 3-dot overflow. The 'no tooltip' point is also true — the adjacent stats IconButton at lines 83-87 sets tooltip:'الإحصائيات' while this PopupMenuButton sets none (Flutter does still supply a default localized 'show menu' tooltip, so it's not literally inaccessible to screen readers). I downgraded high→medium because this is an information-architecture/discoverability concern, not a functional defect: navigation works, every item has a clear Arabic label once opened, and an overflow menu for secondary actions is a recognized Material idiom. Real and worth fixing (surface as cards / add tooltip + leading icons), but nothing is broken and all features remain reachable, which does not warrant high severity.

title: Search requires manual submit and offers no auto/debounced search
description: Search only runs when the user presses Enter or taps the arrow_forward button (_submitSearch). Typing does nothing but rebuild the suffix (onChanged: (_) => setState(() {})). The hint even has to instruct the user ('ابحث في القرآن (ثم اضغط Enter)...'). Combined with a second suffix IconButton (arrow_forward) next to the clear button, the search affordance is cramped and non-obvious on a touch-first Arabic app.
impact: Users expect search-as-you-type in a modern app; many will type a query, see nothing happen, and assume search is broken. The parenthetical Enter instruction in the hint is a usability smell. Two side-by-side suffix icons (clear + submit) are easy to mis-tap on mobile.
recommendation: Add debounced live search (e.g. 300-400ms) on onChanged so results appear as the user types, and drop the explicit submit button (or keep Enter as a shortcut). Remove the 'ثم اضغط Enter' instruction from the hint.
evidence: hintText: 'ابحث في القرآن (ثم اضغط Enter)...', ... onChanged: (_) => setState(() {}), onSubmitted: _submitSearch

verdict.reasoning: Every piece of cited evidence is accurate in lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart. Line 134 hint text is literally 'ابحث في القرآن (ثم اضغط Enter)...', explicitly telling the user to press Enter. Line 155 onChanged: (_) => setState(() {}) only rebuilds to toggle the conditional clear button (line 139) and does NOT trigger any search. Line 156 onSubmitted: _submitSearch and the arrow_forward IconButton (lines 147-151) are the only paths that set _submittedQuery (lines 65-72), and _submittedQuery is the sole trigger for ref.watch(quranSearchProvider) at lines 104-106. So search is genuinely gated behind explicit submit with no auto/debounced typing search. The suffixIcon at lines 136-153 is indeed a Row cramming the clear button plus the arrow submit button into one slot. The flaw is real and the recommendation is sound. However, 'high' overstates it: manual-submit search is a defensible, widely-used design choice here because quranSearchProvider (search_provider.dart) calls repository.search() which hits a remote API (Quran.com -> AlQuran Cloud -> FTS5 fallback) and already enforces searchMinLength; live search per keystroke would add load and is a known tradeoff. Nothing is broken — Enter, the arrow button, and the hint all let the user complete a search; there is no crash, data loss, or navigation failure. The 'ثم اضغط Enter' hint and the dual-icon suffix are legitimate UX smells worth fixing, but this is a friction/improvement issue, not a high-severity defect. Medium is the accurate rating.

title: Submitting a 1-character query shows misleading 'no results' instead of a min-length hint
description: _submitSearch only checks isEmpty; any non-empty value sets _submittedQuery. But quranSearchProvider returns [] for queries shorter than searchMinLength (=2). So submitting a single character makes the UI render the empty-results state 'لا توجد نتائج لهذا البحث', which is wrong — the search simply wasn't performed.
impact: A user searching a single Arabic letter is told there are no matching verses, which is false and confusing. It hides the real reason (query too short).
recommendation: In _submitSearch, treat value.length < searchMinLength like empty (don't set _submittedQuery) or show an explicit 'أدخل حرفين على الأقل' message instead of the no-results state.
evidence: if (value.isEmpty) { setState(() => _submittedQuery = ''); return; } setState(() => _submittedQuery = value);  // vs provider: if (trimmed.length < searchMinLength) return [];

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed against the actual code. In lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart, _submitSearch (lines 65-72) trims the input and, for any non-empty value (including a single character), executes setState(() => _submittedQuery = value) with no length check. The build method then watches quranSearchProvider(_submittedQuery) because _submittedQuery.isNotEmpty (line 104-106), and renders the search results via _buildSearchSlivers (line 177). The provider at lib/features/home/providers/search_provider.dart:9 short-circuits with `if (trimmed.length < searchMinLength) return [];` where searchMinLength=2 (lib/core/constants/app_constants.dart:14) — so for a 1-char query it returns an empty list WITHOUT ever calling repository.search. _buildSearchSlivers' data branch (line 208) treats results.isEmpty as a real empty result and renders 'لا توجد نتائج لهذا البحث' (line 212). Net effect: a 1-character submitted query shows the misleading 'no results' state even though the search was never performed. Cited lines, evidence quotes, and provider logic all match exactly. Severity is medium (arguably low): the message is genuinely misleading (it implies the search ran and found nothing), but a 1-char query is an uncommon edge case that the user can self-correct by typing more; no data loss or blocked functionality.

title: Loading skeleton replaces the entire screen, hiding search and header cards
description: While chaptersProvider is loading, the whole body is replaced by ChapterListSkeleton. The search field, daily verse card, and continue-reading card are all absent during loading and only pop in once chapters resolve, causing a jarring layout shift. The skeleton also has fixed itemCount: 10 and NeverScrollableScrollPhysics, so it shows a static block unrelated to the real 114-row list.
impact: On a slow/cold start the user sees only grey bars, cannot start typing a search, and then experiences a full-screen content jump when data arrives. Feels broken/empty rather than 'loading'.
recommendation: Keep the search field (and ideally the header cards) mounted during loading and only skeleton the chapter list region, so the screen is stable and interactive while chapters load.
evidence: loading: () => const ChapterListSkeleton(),  // ChapterListSkeleton: physics: NeverScrollableScrollPhysics, itemCount: 10

verdict.reasoning: Verified against both cited files. In lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart, the entire Scaffold body (line 102) is `chaptersAsync.when(...)`. The search TextField (lines 130-157), DailyVerseCard, and ContinueReadingCard (lines 119-122) are all built ONLY inside the `data:` branch's CustomScrollView. Line 192 is exactly `loading: () => const ChapterListSkeleton(),`, so during the loading state none of these elements are mounted — only the skeleton renders. lib/features/home/widgets/chapter_skeleton.dart confirms ChapterListSkeleton uses `physics: const NeverScrollableScrollPhysics()` (line 17) and `itemCount: 10` (line 18), producing 10 static gray boxes unrelated to the real 114-chapter list. When chapters resolve, the screen swaps from that 10-box block to a CustomScrollView that newly inserts the search field and two header cards above 114 tiles — a genuine layout shift, and the search box is non-interactive while loading. chaptersProvider is a FutureProvider calling repository.getChapters(), which is network-first per the 3-tier fallback, so the loading state is observably visible on cold start of the app's landing screen, not a sub-frame flicker. Every cited detail (line number, body-replacement behavior, physics, itemCount) is accurate. Severity medium is appropriate: real UX/stability defect (content jump, search unavailable during load) but not crash- or data-level.

title: Search clear button visibility can desync from controller text
description: The clear IconButton renders only `if (_searchController.text.isNotEmpty)`, but the only thing that rebuilds on text change is `onChanged: (_) => setState(() {})`. Any programmatic text change (e.g. future autofill/paste handlers) or a rebuild triggered by other state would not be guaranteed in sync; more concretely, the suffix Row always reserves space for the submit button while the clear button appears/disappears, shifting the submit icon horizontally as the user types.
impact: The submit (arrow) icon jumps sideways the moment the first character is typed because the clear icon appears to its right inside the Row, making the tap target move under the user's finger.
recommendation: Drive the suffix from a ValueListenableBuilder on the controller (not ad-hoc setState), and keep the submit button position stable (e.g. fixed-width clear slot or AnimatedOpacity) so it doesn't shift when the clear icon toggles.
evidence: suffixIcon: Row(... children: [ if (_searchController.text.isNotEmpty) IconButton(icon: Icon(Icons.clear) ...), IconButton(icon: Icon(Icons.arrow_forward_rounded) ...) ])

verdict.reasoning:
The cited code at lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart:136-155 matches the evidence exactly. The claim has two parts and only one holds up.

PART 1 (the title's "desync from controller text"): NOT a real present bug. Every code path that mutates _searchController triggers a rebuild — onChanged: setState({}) at line 155 covers all typing, and the clear button's _searchController.clear() (line 143) is immediately paired with setState (line 144). Grep confirms the controller is only read in _submitSearch and only written by the clear button; there is NO autofill/paste handler. The claim itself hedges with "future autofill/paste handlers" and "rebuild triggered by other state," i.e. it speculates about non-existent code. So the headline desync concern is invalid for the actual codebase.

PART 2 (the "more concretely" layout shift): REAL and code-grounded. suffixIcon is Row(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [if(_searchController.text.isNotEmpty) clearBtn, submitBtn]). The submit IconButton is always the last child; the clear IconButton is conditionally inserted before it. The Row sizes to content (min) and is anchored at the field's trailing edge by InputDecorator. When the text goes empty→non-empty (or is cleared), the Row's width changes by one IconButton width, so the submit icon's absolute screen position shifts horizontally as the user types the first character or clears. App is wrapped in Directionality(rtl) per app.dart:56-57, but the shift occurs regardless of direction. This is a genuine, observable UI jitter.

Net: the flaw exists, but it is a minor cosmetic icon-shift, not a functional defect, and the title's framing (controller desync) is the speculative/incorrect part. Severity medium is overstated; downgrading to low. The accurate, narrower issue is the conditional clear button inside the MainAxisSize.min suffix Row causing the submit icon to move.

title: Hardcoded amber/Color(0xFFD97706) bypasses theme tokens (breaks AMOLED/sepia/dark consistency)
description: The daily verse card, continue-reading card, chapter tile, and search-result tile all hardcode Colors.amber.* and const Color(0xFFD97706) instead of theme.colorScheme / appAccentColor. The daily-verse loading shimmer also hardcodes a white container (color: Colors.white) regardless of theme.
impact: On AMOLED (pure black) and sepia themes these amber tints and the white shimmer block clash with the surface, and any future accent-color change won't propagate. The white shimmer container flashes bright on dark/AMOLED screens.
recommendation: Replace literal amber / 0xFFD97706 with the centralized accent token (appAccentColor / theme tokens) and use a theme-derived surface color for the shimmer container instead of Colors.white.
evidence: colors: [Colors.amber.withValues(alpha: 0.08), ...], ... color: Colors.amber[700], ... loading shimmer: Container(... color: Colors.white ...)

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the cited file in full. lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart hardcodes Colors.amber.* for the gradient (L37-39), border (L43), header icon/text (L52,59), copy/share icons (L64,76), and chapter label (L131), instead of the existing centralized token appAccentColor (theme_constants.dart:122) or theme.colorScheme. The loading shimmer at L147 hardcodes color: Colors.white, which flashes a white 160px block on dark/AMOLED/sepia backgrounds. The broader claim is also verified: continue_reading_card.dart (L53-113) hardcodes Colors.amber.* plus const Color(0xFFD97706) at L96, and home_screen.dart (chapter tiles/search) hardcodes Color(0xFFD97706)/Colors.amber at L251,352,362,376. The flaw is real because the theme layer (app_theme.dart) defines a DIFFERENT accent for AMOLED (appAccentColorAmoled = 0xFFFFB74D, theme_constants.dart:124), so these literal-amber widgets will not match the theme accent in AMOLED, and the white shimmer ignores theme surface entirely. Not a Flutter idiom issue and not handled by the RTL/Directionality wrapper (which only affects layout direction, not color). Severity medium is correct: cosmetic/consistency rather than functional, but the white-on-black shimmer is a clearly visible glitch.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart:37-147 (cited 37-83 is accurate but the Colors.white shimmer flaw is at line 147)

title: Daily verse share/copy uses textUthmani but reader/translation use settings font — Arabic font inconsistency in card
description: The daily verse Arabic text uses fontFamily: settings.quranFont, but the search-result tiles in home_screen.dart hardcode fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New' and the chapter name uses fontFamily: 'Amiri'. So the same Arabic Quran content renders in three different fonts across the home surface depending on where it appears, none of which respect a single source of truth.
impact: Visual inconsistency: a verse shown in the daily card looks different from the same verse shown in search results, and the user's chosen quranFont is honored in one place but ignored in another. Inconsistent typography undermines a Quran app's core presentation.
recommendation: Use settings.quranFont for all Arabic Quran text (daily card, search results, chapter names where appropriate) so the user's font choice is consistent everywhere.
evidence: daily card: fontFamily: settings.quranFont  // search tile: fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New'  // chapter tile: fontFamily: 'Amiri'

verdict.reasoning: Verified against actual code. The daily verse card renders the Quran verse text (verse.textUthmani) with fontFamily: settings.quranFont (lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart:103). The home screen's search-result tile renders the same content type — a verse's Arabic text (result.text) — but hardcodes fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New' (lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart:260). This is a genuine inconsistency: settings.quranFont is the established single source of truth for Quran verse text everywhere else in the app (reader verse_card.dart, mushaf_view.dart, memorization, share_sheet, tafsir_sheet, chapter_header all use it; default value is 'Hafs Smart' per settings_local_datasource.dart:16 and settings_provider.dart:40). So even a user on defaults sees the daily verse in Hafs Smart but search results in Scheherazade New, and a user who picks Amiri/Hafs sees their choice ignored in search. Real, observable, code-grounded — though minor (search is a transient surface), so low severity stands. Two caveats reduce the claim's framing: (1) the third 'font' is chapter.nameArabic with fontFamily: 'Amiri' (home_screen.dart:393), which is a SURAH NAME/title, not verse content — styling a heading in a distinct display font is a legitimate design choice, so the 'same Quran content in three fonts' framing is overstated for that case; the real inconsistency is the two-way daily-card-vs-search-tile divergence. (2) The CLAIM's File/Line field points only to the daily card; the search-tile and chapter-tile evidence actually lives in home_screen.dart.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart:260 (search-result verse text hardcodes 'Scheherazade New' instead of settings.quranFont); compare lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart:103 (uses settings.quranFont). Chapter name at home_screen.dart:393 ('Amiri') is a title, not verse content.

title: Auto-resume pushes reader on startup with no way to cancel, can fight back-navigation
description: On first build, if autoResumeLastAyah is on and a last session exists, the app immediately context.pushNamed('reader') in a post-frame callback. There is no confirmation and no prompt; the user lands directly in the reader every launch. The guard _startupResumeHandled is a static bool, so it persists across HomeScreen instance recreations for the process lifetime, but the push itself happens before the user can interact with Home.
impact: Users who want to browse the index on launch are forced into the reader and must press back every time. With the global RTL Directionality and the reader's own back affordance, this auto-push can feel like the app 'won't stay' on Home.
recommendation: Replace the silent auto-push with a non-intrusive resume affordance (the ContinueReadingCard already exists for this), or gate the auto-push so it only fires on a true cold start and offer a visible way to disable it.
evidence: WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) => _handleStartupResume()); ... context.pushNamed('reader', pathParameters: {'chapterId': session.chapterId.toString()}, ...)

verdict.reasoning: The cited code exists exactly as described. home_screen.dart:31 registers a post-frame callback in initState that runs _handleStartupResume() (lines 40-63). That method reads settings.autoResumeLastAyah (default true, confirmed in settings_provider.dart:47 and settings_local_datasource.dart:61), fetches the last session, and at lines 54-62 calls context.pushNamed('reader', ...) with no confirmation/prompt. The static _startupResumeHandled bool (line 26) does persist for the process lifetime. So the core flaw -- silent auto-push into the reader on every cold start where a session exists, with no in-context way to cancel -- is real. However, two qualifiers reduce severity: (1) The static guard is set to true at line 42 BEFORE the push, so once back-navigated to Home the callback never re-fires; back navigation works normally. The title's 'can fight back-navigation' is therefore inaccurate/overstated -- there is no navigation loop. (2) A user-facing toggle exists (reading_section.dart:154-159 'استئناف آخر موضع عند الفتح') so users can disable it, and the ContinueReadingCard (continue_reading_card.dart) already offers a non-intrusive resume tap target, making the auto-push redundant. Auto-resume-on-launch is a common, defensible reading-app pattern that is opt-out. Net: a legitimate but mild UX/navigation concern, not a defect; medium overstates it given it fires only once per process, back works, and it's user-disableable.

title: Empty search-results state forces full-height SliverFillRemaining, hiding the rest of the page
description: When a search yields no results, the slivers return a SliverFillRemaining(hasScrollBody: false) centering 'لا توجد نتائج لهذا البحث'. Because the search field sliver above it has a fixed height, the empty message gets vertically centered in the remaining viewport, leaving a large empty gap and pushing the message far from the search box that produced it.
impact: The no-results message floats in the middle of an otherwise blank screen, disconnected from the query, which reads as a layout glitch rather than a helpful empty state.
recommendation: Render the empty-results message as a normal SliverToBoxAdapter with modest top padding directly under the results header, optionally with a suggestion to refine the query.
evidence: SliverFillRemaining(hasScrollBody: false, child: Center(child: Text('لا توجد نتائج لهذا البحث')))

verdict.reasoning: The cited code at lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart:208-214 matches the evidence exactly: when search results are empty, _buildSearchSlivers returns const [SliverFillRemaining(hasScrollBody: false, child: Center(child: Text('لا توجد نتائج لهذا البحث')))]. The layout claim is correct. During an active search (_submittedQuery non-empty), the DailyVerseCard/ContinueReadingCard block at lines 114-126 is skipped, so above the empty-state sliver there is only the small search-field sliver (~60-70px, lines 127-159) and the small 'نتائج البحث' header sliver (lines 160-175). SliverFillRemaining with hasScrollBody:false sizes its child to fill the remaining viewport extent, and the wrapping Center then vertically centers the Text within that large extent. The result is exactly as described: the message is centered in most of the screen height, leaving a big empty gap and pushing it far from the search box that produced it. This is real and code-grounded, not speculation, and nothing in the RTL Directionality wrapper, theme, or Scaffold mitigates it. Severity 'low' is correct: it is purely cosmetic, only affects the no-results path, the message stays visible, and centering an empty-state can even be a deliberate pattern in some apps — so user impact is minor. The recommendation (SliverToBoxAdapter with top padding directly under the header) is a reasonable fix.

title: ContinueReadingCard parses verseKey unsafely with int.parse(split(':')[1])
description: The card displays the verse number via int.parse(verseKey.split(':')[1]). If verseKey is ever malformed, lacks a ':', or is an unexpected format from a stored session, split(':')[1] throws RangeError or int.parse throws FormatException, and the exception is raised during build (not inside the AsyncValue.error path), crashing the card / home screen.
impact: A corrupted or legacy verseKey in persisted progress would throw during widget build on the Home screen, potentially red-screening the main screen with no recovery.
recommendation: Use a safe parse (e.g. int.tryParse on the trailing segment with a length check, or reuse formatVerseReference from arabic_utils which already guards parts.length != 2) and fall back gracefully.
evidence: '${chapter.nameArabic} • آية ${toArabicNumeral(int.parse(verseKey.split(':')[1]))}'

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed at lib/features/home/widgets/continue_reading_card.dart:75, exactly as cited: `'${chapter.nameArabic} • آية ${toArabicNumeral(int.parse(verseKey.split(':')[1]))}'`. This runs in the synchronous build body inside the `data:` branch of `chaptersAsync.when`, so any exception here is NOT caught by the `error:` branch (which only handles the AsyncValue's own error) and would propagate to a red error widget / crash the card on the home screen. The two unguarded operations are real: `verseKey.split(':')[1]` throws RangeError for a string with no ':' (e.g. ''), and `int.parse` throws FormatException for a non-numeric second segment.\n\nHOWEVER, the likelihood is low, which is why I downgrade from medium to low. `verseKey` reaching this line is always a non-null String: ReaderSession.fromJson (reader_session.dart:47) defaults null to '1:1', ReadingProgress.lastVerseKey is a required non-null String, and both deserializers (progress_local_datasource.dart:33,60) wrap in try/catch that discards type-mismatch errors. Every in-app writer produces the controlled format '$chapterId:$verseNumber' (reader_screen.dart, alquran_cloud_datasource.dart:56), which always contains ':' and a numeric tail. So a malformed-but-non-null verseKey is only reachable via corrupted/tampered SharedPreferences or a legacy schema — there is no live code path that triggers the crash today. It is a genuine defensive-coding gap, made more glaring because the same file's sibling code already does it safely: updateProgress uses `int.tryParse(verseKey.split(':').last) ?? 0` (progress_provider.dart:57) and arabic_utils.formatVerseReference guards `parts.length != 2` and uses int.tryParse (arabic_utils.dart:23-30). The recommendation (use tryParse / reuse formatVerseReference) is valid. Real latent bug, but low severity due to no reachable trigger in current code.

title: Daily verse copy/share icons are tiny (16px) sub-minimum tap targets
description: The copy and share IconButtons use 16px icons with padding: EdgeInsets.zero and constraints minWidth/minHeight: 32 — below the 48x48 minimum recommended touch target. Their color is amber at alpha 0.6, giving low contrast against the faint amber gradient background.
impact: Hard to tap accurately (especially for users with motor or vision impairment) and visually faint, so the copy/share actions on the daily verse are easy to miss or mis-hit.
recommendation: Increase tap targets to at least 48x48 (default IconButton constraints) and raise icon contrast (remove the alpha 0.6 or use the accent token at full opacity).
evidence: IconButton(icon: Icon(Icons.copy, size: 16, color: Colors.amber[600]?.withValues(alpha: 0.6)), padding: EdgeInsets.zero, constraints: const BoxConstraints(minWidth: 32, minHeight: 32))

verdict.reasoning: Verified against lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart. The copy IconButton (lines 63-74) and share IconButton (lines 75-83) both use Icon(..., size: 16, color: Colors.amber[600]?.withValues(alpha: 0.6)), padding: EdgeInsets.zero, and constraints: const BoxConstraints(minWidth: 32, minHeight: 32). The 32x32 constraint explicitly overrides Flutter's default IconButton 48x48 (Material minimum) touch target, so these are genuine sub-minimum tap targets. The amber[600] at alpha 0.6 sits on a very faint amber gradient (alpha 0.08 -> 0.03), confirming the low-contrast claim. The cited evidence and line range (63-83) match the code exactly. Nothing in the theme, RTL Directionality wrapper, or any default mitigates this — the constraints are hardcoded smaller than the default. Severity 'low' is correct: these are secondary convenience actions (copy/share) and the verse text itself is also tappable, so impact is limited to users with motor/visual impairments rather than blocking core flow.

title: Daily verse card silently disappears on error/null with no feedback
description: Both the null-data case (data == null) and the error case return const SizedBox.shrink(), so on any failure the entire 'آية اليوم' card vanishes with no message or retry. The user sees a smaller header area with no indication anything was supposed to be there.
impact: A failed daily-verse fetch (e.g. offline on first run before bundle resolves) silently removes a headline feature; the user can't tell if it's broken or simply absent, and has no way to retry.
recommendation: Show a compact fallback (e.g. a static bundled verse, or a small 'تعذر تحميل آية اليوم' with a retry) instead of collapsing to nothing on error.
evidence: if (data == null) return const SizedBox.shrink(); ... error: (_, __) => const SizedBox.shrink(),

verdict.reasoning: The cited code is exact. Line 23: `if (data == null) return const SizedBox.shrink();` and line 152: `error: (_, __) => const SizedBox.shrink(),` both match verbatim. The provider (daily_verse_provider.dart) reinforces this: it returns null on a missing verse (line 29) and swallows all exceptions returning null (lines 35-37, `catch (_) { return null; }`), so realistically the .when() error branch rarely fires and the null branch is the common failure path — but BOTH collapse the card. In home_screen.dart line 120, DailyVerseCard sits in a Column above a SizedBox(height:12) spacer and ContinueReadingCard, so on failure the 'آية اليوم' card silently vanishes and the elements below shift up with no message, placeholder, or retry. The described user impact is real. Severity 'low' is correct: the daily verse is a non-essential, decorative supplement, the failure requires the repository's 3-tier fallback to fully fail (rare), and silently hiding optional content on failure is a defensible/common Flutter idiom rather than an outright bug. So it is a legitimate-but-minor UX gap, partly opinion (preferred fallback behavior) but grounded in real code with a real, if small, consequence.

title: No font-size control in the reader screen
description: The reader AppBar exposes only tajweed legend, view-mode toggle, and chapter audio. There is no way to increase/decrease Arabic font size from within the reading experience, even though font size is the single most-used reading control and is stored per-app (settingsProvider.setFontSize, range 18-48sp). To change text size the user must back out of the reader, open Settings, adjust the slider, and re-enter. Both flowing (VerseCard) and mushaf (_MushafPageContent uses settings.fontSize) modes read settings.fontSize but offer no in-context A+/A- affordance.
impact: Reading comfort (font size) is the most frequently adjusted setting while reading, yet it requires leaving the screen entirely. Older users and anyone fine-tuning legibility face a multi-screen round-trip for every adjustment.
recommendation: Add inline font-size +/- IconButtons (or a quick popup slider) to the reader AppBar that call ref.read(settingsProvider.notifier).setFontSize(...), clamped to the 18-48 range. Reflect changes live in both flowing and mushaf modes.
evidence: actions: [ if (settings.showTajweed) IconButton(...palette...), IconButton(...view_list/auto_stories...), _ChapterAudioButton(...) ]  // no font-size control

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual code. reader_screen.dart lines 352-374 define the AppBar `actions` with exactly three items: a conditional tajweed-legend IconButton (Icons.palette_outlined), the view-mode toggle IconButton (view_list/auto_stories), and _ChapterAudioButton. There is no font-size affordance. A grep across the entire lib/features/reader directory for setFontSize, text_increase/text_decrease, A+/A-, or a font slider returns nothing; the reader's only GestureDetectors are for verse-tap/tafsir (verse_card.dart:239) and mushaf navigation (mushaf_view.dart:208,269), and the only Slider is the audio scrubber (audio_player_bar.dart:45). The sole setFontSize caller in the codebase is the Settings screen (reading_section.dart:45), confirming the user must leave the reader, open Settings, adjust the slider, and return. Both reading modes consume settings.fontSize live — VerseCard flowing mode (verse_card.dart:49,74,102,127,143) and mushaf _MushafPageContent (mushaf_view.dart:448,463,477) — so the proposed inline +/- control is technically viable and would reflect in both. setFontSize persists via the data source, and the 18-48 range is confirmed (fontSizeMin=18, fontSizeMax=48 in constants). Every factual assertion in the claim is accurate. I downgraded severity from high to medium: this is a missing in-context convenience affordance for which a working (if clunky) path exists via Settings, not a broken, data-losing, or blocking defect. It is real, user-impacting friction for the single most-used reading control, but does not rise to high.

title: Mushaf mode ignores tajweed/translation settings and over-fetches whole chapters
description: mushafPageVersesProvider calls repository.getVerses(ch) with no arguments, so withTajweed/withWords/translationIds are never passed. In flowing mode versesProvider passes settings.activeTranslationIds, showWordByWord, showTajweed. Result: enabling 'showTajweed' colors verses in flowing mode but mushaf mode renders plain text (it draws verse.textUthmani directly with no tajweed spans). Additionally, for every chapter on the page it fetches the chapter's ENTIRE verse list and filters client-side, so a page in Al-Baqarah pulls all 286 verses to show ~15.
impact: Tajweed coloring silently does nothing in mushaf mode, an inconsistency users will notice when toggling modes. The full-chapter fetch wastes memory/CPU on every page swipe, hurting scroll smoothness on large surahs.
recommendation: Pass withTajweed: settings.showTajweed (read via ref) into getVerses for mushaf, and render tajweed spans when present. Prefer a verse-range fetch (by verseKey range) instead of loading entire chapters and filtering.
evidence: for (var ch = page.startChapterId; ch <= page.endChapterId; ch++) { final chapterVerses = await repository.getVerses(ch); ... }  // no settings, full chapter pulled

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual code. (1) Tajweed/settings not passed: lib/features/reader/providers/mushaf_provider.dart:24 calls repository.getVerses(ch) with NO named args, so withTajweed/withWords/translationIds fall to the defaults in quran_repository.dart:41-43 (translationIds [16], withWords false, withTajweed false). By contrast lib/features/reader/providers/reader_provider.dart:9-14 explicitly passes settings.activeTranslationIds, settings.showWordByWord, settings.showTajweed. (2) Mushaf renders plain text: lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart:444-445 emits a TextSpan with text: verse.textUthmani and never uses verse.textUthmaniTajweed or a TajweedText widget, so enabling showTajweed colors verses in flowing mode (verse_card uses TajweedText) but mushaf stays plain. Confirmed real and user-visible. (3) Over-fetch: mushaf_provider.dart:23-43 loops startChapterId..endChapterId calling getVerses(ch) (whole chapter) then filters client-side; fetchVerses has no verse-range variant on any tier (quran_remote_datasource by_chapter, alquran_cloud_datasource /surah/$chapterId, local getVersesByChapter), so a Baqarah page pulls all 286 verses for ~15. Real but mitigated: the remote datasource caches per chapter (quran_remote_datasource.dart:46-47), so it is a one-time-per-chapter cost. Adjusting severity high->medium because (a) translations are never displayed in mushaf mode at all, so the 'translationIds not passed' sub-point has zero visible effect — only the tajweed-not-rendering point is genuinely user-facing, and (b) the over-fetch is cached/amortized rather than per-page-repeated. The core defect (showTajweed ignored in mushaf mode) is real and correctly located.

title: Mushaf verse highlight never clears and re-applies on every revisit to the page
description: Every _MushafPageContent is built with widget.highlightVerseKey (the original highlightVerseKey passed once into ReaderScreen and forwarded unchanged). The highlighted verse gets a persistent amber background (Color(0xFFD97706).withValues(alpha:0.15)) on both the verse text and its ayah marker. Because the key is never reset after the initial scroll, the highlight stays painted on that verse for the entire session, and every time the user swipes back to that page it re-highlights and re-attempts an auto-scroll.
impact: A verse the user navigated to (e.g. from search/bookmark) stays visually marked indefinitely with no way to dismiss it, and returning to the page yanks the scroll position to that verse unexpectedly.
recommendation: Clear the highlight after the first successful scroll (e.g. null it out via a callback/provider once consumed), or scope the highlight to the initial page only so swiping away and back does not re-trigger scroll/highlight.
evidence: return _MushafPageContent(page: page, pageNumber: pageNumber, highlightVerseKey: widget.highlightVerseKey);  // same key on every page, never cleared

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed against the code. `highlightVerseKey` originates as the immutable `widget.highlightVerseKey` on ReaderScreen, is passed once into MushafPageView (reader_screen.dart:535), and is forwarded unchanged to every `_MushafPageContent` (mushaf_view.dart:197). It is never reset anywhere — no setState/provider/callback clears it. Highlight persistence is real: `_MushafPageContentState.build` computes `isHighlighted` purely from `verse.verseKey == widget.highlightVerseKey` (lines 441-442) and paints the amber background `Color(0xFFD97706).withValues(alpha:0.15)` on both the verse text (451-453) and the ayah marker (465-467), so the tint stays on that verse for the whole mushaf session.

Re-scroll-on-revisit is also real. `_MushafPageContent` is built inside a plain `PageView.builder` (lines 175-200) with NO key on the child, NO AutomaticKeepAlive/wantKeepAlive/PageStorage (grep confirms none in lib/features/reader). So when a page scrolls past the PageView cache extent and is swiped back to, a fresh `_MushafPageContentState` is created with `_hasScrolledToHighlight=false`. With `highlightIndex>=0`, the guard at line 408 (`!_hasScrolledToHighlight`) passes and a postFrameCallback re-runs `Scrollable.ensureVisible` (400ms animation, alignment 0.3) at lines 408-430, re-centering the highlighted verse and fighting the user's scroll position. The flaw exists exactly as described.

Severity medium is correct: it is a genuine recurring UX annoyance (permanent tint + unsolicited auto-scroll on every revisit), but the tint is subtle (0.15 alpha) and there is no crash, data loss, or functional breakage. Not high.

Minor location note: the cited line 196-198 correctly points to the forwarding site that is the root cause, but the observable flaw is implemented in the `_MushafPageContentState` body.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart:197 (root cause: forwarding of widget.highlightVerseKey); flaw manifests at 403-430 (re-scroll guard reset per page rebuild) and 441-467 (persistent highlight paint)

title: Mushaf 'page' is a free scroll view, breaking one-page fidelity
description: _MushafPageContent wraps the page text in a SingleChildScrollView. A traditional mushaf page is a fixed unit; making each page independently vertically scrollable means content can overflow and scroll within a 'page', and the floating page-number pill (Positioned bottom:16) sits over scrollable text. With large font sizes a single mushaf page no longer corresponds to a real mushaf page, undermining the entire purpose of mushaf mode (consistent page numbers / memorization by page position).
impact: Users relying on mushaf page layout for memorization or cross-referencing lose the fixed-page guarantee; text reflows and scrolls arbitrarily, and the page indicator overlaps content.
recommendation: Render mushaf pages with FittedBox/auto-scaled text to fit the viewport (or cap font scaling in mushaf mode) so each page is a non-scrolling fixed unit, and reserve space for the page indicator instead of overlaying it.
evidence: child: SingleChildScrollView(controller: _scrollController, child: Column( ... buildVerseSpans(verses) ... ))

verdict.reasoning: All four sub-claims verified against the actual code in lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart. (1) The page content IS wrapped in a SingleChildScrollView at lines 486-487, exactly matching the cited evidence, fed by a per-page ScrollController (line 353). (2) Each _MushafPageContentState owns its own scroll controller, so every mushaf 'page' is independently vertically scrollable. (3) The verse text uses settings.fontSize.toDouble() directly (lines 448, 463, 477) with height:2.0 and forceStrutHeight, and there is NO FittedBox/BoxFit/scaling/cap anywhere in this widget. The user-facing font range is 18-48 (confirmed in theme_constants.dart / app_constants.dart; default 28). At the upper end, a dense full-page Uthmani layout will exceed viewport height and scroll, so 'page N' stops corresponding to a real mushaf page boundary -- directly undermining mushaf mode's memorization-by-page-position purpose. (4) The page-number pill (Positioned bottom:16, lines 203-232) is a Stack sibling of the PageView, so it floats over the scrolling text rather than reserving layout space (the bottom:48 padding only pads within the scroll body). This is a genuine design-fidelity/UX flaw, not Flutter idiom and not handled by the RTL/Directionality wrapper (that only fixes swipe direction). It degrades gracefully at default size, which is why medium (not high) is the correct rating.

title: Page-jump dialog mixes Arabic-Indic and Western digits and rejects Arabic input
description: The page indicator displays Arabic-Indic numerals via toArabicNumeral(_currentPage), and the jump dialog hint is Arabic-Indic ('١ - ٦٠٤'), but the suffixText is Western ('/ 604'), the TextField is forced TextDirection.ltr, prefilled with Western '$_currentPage', and parsing uses int.tryParse which only accepts Western digits. A user who reads '٦٠٤' on the pill and types Arabic-Indic digits gets silently rejected (tryParse returns null, nothing happens, dialog stays open with no error).
impact: Inconsistent numeral systems confuse Arabic users; typing the numerals they actually see fails silently with no feedback, making the page-jump feature feel broken.
recommendation: Use Arabic-Indic consistently (suffix and prefill), normalize Arabic-Indic digits to Western before parsing (or accept both), and show inline validation feedback when input is out of range instead of silently doing nothing.
evidence: hintText: '١ - ٦٠٤', suffixText: '/ 604', ... text: '$_currentPage', ... final page = int.tryParse(val);  // rejects ٦٠٤

verdict.reasoning: Every cited fact is confirmed by the actual code in lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart. The page pill renders Arabic-Indic numerals via toArabicNumeral(_currentPage) (line 223). Inside _showPageJumpDialog: the prefill is Western via text: '$_currentPage' (line 59); the TextField is forced TextDirection.ltr (line 68); hintText is Arabic-Indic '١ - ٦٠٤' (line 70) while suffixText is Western '/ 604' (line 71) — a genuine, visible digit-script inconsistency. Both submit paths parse with int.tryParse (lines 75 and 89). Dart's int.tryParse only accepts ASCII/Western digits and returns null for Arabic-Indic digits (U+0660–U+0669); there is no digit-normalization helper anywhere in arabic_utils.dart (only toArabicNumeral exists, which goes the other direction). So a user primed by the Arabic-Indic pill/hint who types '٦٠٤' gets null, and since neither onSubmitted (lines 74–80) nor the انتقال button (lines 88–94) has an else branch, the dialog silently stays open with no error. The same silent no-feedback also applies to out-of-range Western input (e.g. '700'). The claim's line range 58–99 and all evidence strings match exactly. Severity medium is fair: it is a real, reproducible consistency/UX flaw, but confined to one secondary page-jump dialog (the primary navigation is the bottom sheet), is not a crash or data-loss issue, and the Arabic-digit rejection path additionally depends on the user's keyboard emitting Arabic-Indic numerals.

title: Hardcoded accent color instead of theme/appAccentColor token
description: Mushaf verse highlight, ayah-marker color, and chapter-name header all hardcode Color(0xFFD97706). The project defines appAccentColor in lib/core/constants/theme_constants.dart and even distinct variants for AMOLED (appAccentColorAmoled 0xFFFFB74D) and light (appAccentColorLight). reader_screen.dart's _ChapterAudioButton (lines 701, 710) and chapter_header.dart (line 34) do the same. Because AMOLED uses a lighter accent, the hardcoded #D97706 will be a slightly off / under-contrast amber on the pure-black theme.
impact: Accent color is not theme-aware; on AMOLED the reader's amber differs from the rest of the app's accent, and any future re-theme of the accent won't propagate to the reader.
recommendation: Replace the literal Color(0xFFD97706) usages with appAccentColor (or theme.colorScheme.primary / a theme-resolved accent that respects AMOLED) across mushaf_view.dart, reader_screen.dart, and chapter_header.dart.
evidence: backgroundColor: isHighlighted ? const Color(0xFFD97706).withValues(alpha: 0.15) : null,  ... color: const Color(0xFFD97706),  // ayah marker

verdict.reasoning: Verified against source. lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart hardcodes const Color(0xFFD97706) at line 452 (verse highlight backgroundColor, alpha 0.15), line 464 (ayah-marker text color), line 466 (highlight backgroundColor on marker), and line 508 (chapter-name header text color) — matching the cited evidence exactly. lib/core/constants/theme_constants.dart:122-124 defines appAccentColor=0xFFD97706, appAccentColorLight=0xFFF59E0B, appAccentColorAmoled=0xFFFFB74D. Critically, lib/core/theme/app_theme.dart:186 sets the AMOLED ColorScheme primary to appAccentColorAmoled (0xFFFFB74D), and lines 211/227 use it for nav/focus surfaces. So on AMOLED, theme.colorScheme.primary resolves to the lighter #FFB74D while these hardcoded reader elements remain #D97706 — a genuine, intentional divergence the literal bypasses. The cited sibling occurrences are also confirmed: reader_screen.dart:701 and :710, chapter_header.dart:34. This is a real theme-token/consistency flaw with visible (though cosmetic) AMOLED impact: a slightly darker, lower-contrast, inconsistent amber against pure black versus the rest of the AMOLED-accented UI. Functionally harmless, so medium (not high) is correct; the widespread, repeated pattern keeps it above low.

title: Flowing scroll-to-verse uses crude proportional jump that can mis-target
description: _scrollToVerseRobust estimates the scroll offset as (verseIndex+1)/(verses.length+2) * maxScrollExtent. This assumes uniform verse-card height, which is false (verses vary wildly in length, plus the tall ChapterHeader at index 0). For long surahs the proportional jump lands far from the target, then relies on a single 300ms retry checking currentContext; if the GlobalKey still isn't laid out it recurses up to 5 attempts but each attempt re-applies the same flawed proportional jump. The result is unreliable scroll positioning when deep-linking to a verse via highlightVerseKey.
impact: Opening a specific verse (from search, bookmarks, or saved progress) in flowing mode can land on the wrong part of a long surah, requiring manual scrolling to find the intended verse.
recommendation: Use a ScrollablePositionedList / index-based scroll (e.g. scrollable_positioned_list) to jump precisely to verseIndex, or keep retrying ensureVisible on the GlobalKey after incremental scrolls rather than recomputing the same proportional offset.
evidence: final proportion = targetItem / totalItems; _scrollController.jumpTo((proportion * maxScroll).clamp(0.0, maxScroll));  // assumes uniform heights

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual file. The cited code (lines 230-233) matches the evidence exactly: totalItems = verses.length + 2; targetItem = verseIndex + 1; proportion = targetItem/totalItems; _scrollController.jumpTo((proportion * maxScroll).clamp(...)). This is a pure index-ratio-to-offset estimate that implicitly assumes uniform item heights, which is false: VerseCards vary greatly in height (e.g. short verses vs Ayat al-Kursi 2:255) and index 0 is a tall ChapterHeader (lines 449-454), index verses.length+1 a 100px spacer. The ListView.builder (line 444) uses default cacheExtent (~250px) with no itemExtent/prototypeItem/findChildIndexCallback, so the estimate is genuinely error-prone for long surahs. The retry logic is also correctly described as non-convergent: after the 300ms delay (line 235) if the GlobalKey context is still null, line 248 recurses re-applying the IDENTICAL deterministic jump (proportion*maxScroll is unchanged and the list is unchanged), rather than incrementally scrolling toward the target — so it cannot self-correct when the first jump lands the target outside the build/cacheExtent window. The deep-link path is real and user-facing: app_router.dart:61 passes highlightVerseKey, which flows to _scrollToVerseRobust via the post-frame callback at line 407 (e.g. opening a verse from a bookmark/search). Mitigating nuance the claim slightly understates: a precise Scrollable.ensureVisible (lines 207, 241) IS attempted both up front and after the jump, so when the proportional seek lands the target within cacheExtent (common for short/medium surahs) positioning is corrected accurately; the unreliable behavior is concentrated in long surahs, exactly as described. Real flaw, accurately located, with bounded but genuine UX impact. Medium severity is correct — degrades gracefully to near-target in the common case, no crash, but can mis-target with no convergence guarantee on long surahs. The recommendation (scrollable_positioned_list for index-based jumping) is the standard correct fix.

title: Dead 'hasHighlight' parameter in buildVerseSpans
description: buildVerseSpans declares a named parameter `{bool hasHighlight = false}` and it is passed as true at line 548 for the highlighted verse group, but the parameter is never read inside the function. Highlight styling is instead derived independently per-span by comparing verse.verseKey to widget.highlightVerseKey. The parameter is pure dead code that misleads readers into thinking it controls highlighting.
impact: Misleading API surface; a maintainer may rely on hasHighlight to toggle highlighting and find it has no effect.
recommendation: Remove the unused hasHighlight parameter (and its true argument at the highlight call site), since highlighting is already computed per-verse.
evidence: Widget buildVerseSpans(List<Verse> verseGroup, {bool hasHighlight = false}) { ... }  // hasHighlight never referenced in body

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. The local function buildVerseSpans is declared with `{bool hasHighlight = false}` at lib/features/reader/screens/mushaf_view.dart:434-435. A full grep of the file shows `hasHighlight` appears in exactly two places: the declaration (line 435) and the call-site argument `hasHighlight: true` (line 548). It is never referenced inside the function body (lines 436-482). Highlight styling is instead computed per-span at line 441-442 via `final isHighlighted = widget.highlightVerseKey != null && verse.verseKey == widget.highlightVerseKey;` and applied at lines 451-453 and 465-467. Thus the parameter is truly dead: passing `hasHighlight: true` at line 548 has no effect on rendering, and all four call sites (543, 546-549, 552, 554) behave identically. The cited locations and evidence are accurate. Impact is purely maintainability/clarity (a misleading parameter), with no functional or user-facing effect, so 'low' severity under the Consistency dimension is appropriate.

title: Maintained hardcoded chapter->page table duplicates JSON page data
description: _getInitialMushafPage() hardcodes a 114-entry chapterToPage map as the final fallback for the initial mushaf page. The same mapping is already derivable from quran_pages.json via mushafPageDataSource.getPageForVerse('${chapterId}:1'). This map is a second source of truth that can drift from the bundled page data (it is only reached as a last resort, but several late entries — e.g. surah 81 mapped to 586 alongside 80->585 and 82->587 — are approximate and could disagree with the JSON).
impact: Two divergent page-mapping sources; if the JSON is updated the hardcoded table goes stale, and the fallback may open a slightly wrong page.
recommendation: Drop the hardcoded table and resolve the initial page exclusively through getPageForVerse('${chapterId}:1') (it is already async in _getInitialMushafPageAsync), defaulting to page 1 only on null.
evidence: const chapterToPage = <int, int>{ 1: 1, 2: 2, ... 81: 586, ... }; return chapterToPage[widget.chapterId] ?? 1;

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. reader_screen.dart lines 558-673 define a hardcoded 114-entry `chapterToPage` map returned at line 674 (`return chapterToPage[widget.chapterId] ?? 1;`). It is the final fallback in `_getInitialMushafPageAsync()` (line 328) and is the path actually taken on a fresh chapter open (no session, no highlightVerseKey, no last-flowing-verse). The same data is fully derivable from quran_pages.json via `mushafPageDataSource.getPageForVerse('${chapterId}:1')`, which is already implemented (mushaf_page_datasource.dart lines 68-98) and already used three times in the same async method (lines 312, 318, 324). So this is a genuine duplicated second source of truth and a real maintainability/consistency issue, and the recommended fix is trivially available. One correction to the claim: it implies certain late entries (e.g. surah 81 -> 586) are approximate and 'could disagree' with the JSON. I parsed both sources and computed getPageForVerse for all 114 chapters' first verses — there are zero current mismatches; surah 81 -> 586, 80 -> 585, 82 -> 587 all match the JSON exactly. So there is no present user-visible bug; the risk is purely future drift if the JSON is updated without updating the map. Severity 'low' is appropriate given no current incorrect behavior.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/features/reader/screens/reader_screen.dart:557-675 (map body 558-673, return 674; reached via fallback at line 328)

title: Progress is persisted from a postFrame callback on every flowing build
description: Inside versesAsync.when(data:) the build schedules an addPostFrameCallback that calls _persistReadingPosition on every rebuild of the flowing view (every settings change, bookmark toggle, audio tick, etc.). _persistReadingPosition has a de-dup guard so it usually no-ops, but the postFrame callback and the guard comparisons run on each rebuild, and the verse-card list also rebuilds because ref.watch(bookmarkProvider) is read per-card. This couples persistence to render frequency rather than to actual scroll/position change.
impact: Extra per-frame work in a long ListView; on rapid rebuilds (audio playback updating currentVerseKey) the postFrame scheduling adds avoidable overhead.
recommendation: Move initial-position persistence out of the build/postFrame path (e.g. trigger once via ref.listen on versesProvider or in initState after data resolves), and rely on the ScrollEndNotification handler for ongoing position updates.
evidence: WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) { if (!mounted) return; ... _persistReadingPosition(...); ... });  // inside data: builder, runs every rebuild

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the source. Lines 391-411 of lib/features/reader/screens/reader_screen.dart contain `WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) {...})` inside the `versesAsync.when(data: (verses) {...})` builder, calling `_persistReadingPosition(...)`. This is in the build path, so it runs on every rebuild of the flowing view. The build() method watches settingsProvider (335), audioProvider (342), versesProvider (334), and chaptersProvider (333), so any of these triggers a full rebuild and re-schedules the callback. Critically, audio_provider.dart lines 117-118 update state on every `_player.positionStream` tick (multiple times/second during playback), and since build watches audioProvider, each tick re-runs the data: builder and schedules a fresh postFrame closure plus runs the de-dup guard comparisons (lines 117-121). The per-card `ref.watch(bookmarkProvider)` at lines 486-489 is the screen's ConsumerState ref inside itemBuilder, so bookmark changes also rebuild the whole screen — confirming that claim too. The de-dup guard (lines 117-121) does make the actual SharedPreferences writes no-op unless position changed, so the expensive work is correctly avoided; only the closure allocation, postFrame queueing, and three comparisons run each frame. This is a genuine but minor inefficiency: persistence *scheduling* is coupled to render frequency, not to actual position change. The recommendation is sound — a ScrollEndNotification handler already exists (lines 417-443) for ongoing updates, and initial persistence could move to initState/ref.listen. Severity 'low' is accurate: real coupling, but no user-visible perf impact since the guard prevents redundant I/O.

title: Tool action buttons are below the 48dp minimum tap target
description: _ToolButton wraps a 20px icon in only EdgeInsets.all(8), yielding a tappable area of ~36x36dp (20 + 8 + 8). All five per-verse actions (bookmark, tafsir, share, note, play/pause) use this. Material/WCAG guidance is a minimum touch target of 48x48dp.
impact: Users — especially with motor impairment or large fingers, and on high-DPI phones like the S25 Ultra mentioned in CLAUDE.md — mis-tap adjacent buttons (e.g. hit Share instead of Note since they sit side by side with no separation). The five tightly packed targets make accurate tapping hard.
recommendation: Wrap the Icon in a SizedBox(width: 48, height: 48) / ConstrainedBox with minWidth/minHeight 48, or use IconButton with its built-in constraints, instead of an InkWell+Padding(8).
evidence: child: Padding(padding: const EdgeInsets.all(8), child: Icon(icon, size: 20, ...))

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly against the code. _ToolButton (lib/features/reader/widgets/verse_card.dart:288-306) uses InkWell (NOT IconButton) wrapping Icon(size: 20) in Padding(EdgeInsets.all(8)), giving a tap target of 20 + 8 + 8 = 36x36dp. This is below Material's kMinInteractiveDimension (48.0dp) and WCAG 2.5.5/2.5.8 minimums (44-48dp). Critically, because it's a bare InkWell, none of the built-in IconButton tap-target constraints (which default to 48x48) apply, and there is no ConstrainedBox/SizedBox/MaterialTapTargetSize enforcement anywhere in the tree. The RTL Directionality wrapper and theme do not affect tap-target size, so the flaw is not 'already handled.' The evidence string matches exactly, and all five per-verse actions (bookmark L176, tafsir L182, share L186, note L190, play/pause L195) route through _ToolButton, confirming app-wide scope on the reader screen. Real defect. Downgraded from high to medium: the targets remain functionally usable at 36dp for most users (it's a guideline shortfall, not a functional break), though the five tightly-packed adjacent buttons in a MainAxisAlignment.end Row with no inter-button spacing do compound mis-tap risk, keeping it above low.

title: Tajweed render path drops the forced strut, so line spacing differs from plain mode
description: The default plain-text branch in verse_card builds Text.rich with a StrutStyle(forceStrutHeight: true, height: _lineHeight) to guarantee uniform Arabic line height. TajweedText renders its own Text.rich with NO strutStyle at all — line height comes only from each span's height. Because span heights are driven by mixed-color spans, the effective leading is computed per-line from the tallest span rather than forced, giving visibly different (and uneven) line spacing than the plain mode for the same verse.
impact: Toggling 'showTajweed' visibly changes vertical rhythm and line gaps of the exact same verse, and tajweed lines with tall diacritics can collide. Inconsistent with the carefully forced strut in the plain path.
recommendation: Add the same StrutStyle(forceStrutHeight: true, fontFamily: fontFamily, fontSize: fontSize, height: lineHeight) to the Text.rich inside TajweedText.build().
evidence: return Text.rich(TextSpan(children: spans), textAlign: TextAlign.right, textDirection: TextDirection.rtl);  // no strutStyle

verdict.reasoning: The structural claim is verified. verse_card.dart's plain-text branch (lines 120-146) builds Text.rich WITH strutStyle: StrutStyle(forceStrutHeight: true, fontFamily, fontSize, height: _lineHeight). TajweedText.build() (tajweed_text.dart lines 29-33) builds its Text.rich with NO strutStyle; line height comes only from each span's TextStyle height. mushaf_view.dart (line 474) also forces strut height, so the forced-strut pattern is an established convention and TajweedText is the lone path omitting it. The same _lineHeight is passed to both branches (verse_card line 103). So a genuine consistency gap exists and the recommended one-line fix is correct.\n\nHOWEVER the claim's stated causal mechanism is wrong. It asserts the spacing is uneven 'because span heights are driven by mixed-color spans... computed per-line from the tallest span.' All tajweed spans share identical fontFamily, fontSize, and height (lines 49-53, 66-71, 85-88); only color differs, and color has zero effect on line-box metrics. Therefore spacing WITHIN tajweed mode is uniform, not uneven, and there is no 'tallest span' variation. The real difference is forceStrutHeight:true (clamps line box to height*fontSize) vs span-derived strut. For identical height multipliers these usually render the same; they diverge only on Arabic-tashkeel-heavy lines where natural ascent/descent exceeds the height-scaled box (forced strut clamps, strut-less path expands). That is a subtle, edge-case-dependent divergence, not the 'visibly different and uneven' effect described. Real flaw, correct fix, but cause misdescribed and impact overstated, so severity lowered medium->low.

title: Word-by-word ignores user's lineHeight setting (hardcoded 1.6)

recommendation: Pass the resolved lineHeight from verse_card into WordByWordWidget (as plain/tajweed paths already do) and use it for the Arabic word's height instead of the literal 1.6.
evidence: fontSize: fontSize, height: 1.6,  // hardcoded, not settings.lineHeight

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed in code. verse_card.dart defines `_lineHeight` (lines 35-44) resolving settings.lineHeight to 1.8/2.2/2.8. The plain-text path uses `height: _lineHeight` (line 128) and the tajweed path passes `lineHeight: _lineHeight` to TajweedText (line 103). The word-by-word path (lines 71-78) calls WordByWordWidget without any line-height, and WordByWordWidget's constructor (lines 13-20) has no lineHeight parameter, so the Arabic word Text hardcodes `height: 1.6` (word_by_word_widget.dart line 40). However, severity is overstated as medium: in this widget each word sits in its own single-line Text inside an IntrinsicWidth Column within a Wrap, so `height` only scales that single line's bounding box; inter-word row spacing is governed by `runSpacing: 8`, not by this height. Because the words are single-line, changing line-height has limited visible effect (unlike the multi-line flowing/tajweed paths where leading matters a lot). title: Iqlab and Ikhfa Shafawi are color-coded as 'Ikhfa Meem' — wrong rule mapping vs. legend
description: colorMap maps the Quran.com classes 'iqlab' and 'ikhfa_shafawi' to ikhfaMeemSaakin (light blue), whose only legend entry (arabicLabels['ikhfa_meem']) reads 'إخفاء ميم ساكنة'. TajweedText.colorMap[cssClass] therefore paints these letters a color whose legend name does not describe the actual rule.
impact: A learner consulting the tajweed legend sees a letter highlighted light-blue, looks it up as 'إخفاء ميم ساكنة', and is taught the wrong rule (it is actually Iqlab). The legend cannot explain colors that represent merged/renamed rules, undermining the educational purpose and Darussalam-standard claim.
recommendation: Give iqlab, ikhfa_shafawi, idgham_shafawi, and the madd variants their own colors + legend labels (or at minimum relabel the shared entries to the correct Arabic rule names), so every rendered color has a truthful legend entry.
evidence: 'iqlab': ikhfaMeemSaakin, 'ikhfa_shafawi': ikhfaMeemSaakin,  // legend label is 'إخفاء ميم ساكنة'

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading all three relevant files. In lib/core/constants/theme_constants.dart, colorMap maps 'iqlab' (line 60) and 'ikhfa_shafawi' (line 61) to ikhfaMeemSaakin = Color(0xFF63B3ED), light blue. The ONLY arabicLabels entry tied to that color is 'ikhfa_meem' => 'إخفاء ميم ساكنة' (line 72). In tajweed_text.dart line 61, TajweedColors.colorMap[cssClass] paints an Iqlab/Ikhfa-Shafawi letter that light blue. In tajweed_legend.dart lines 20-23, the legend renders only the 7 arabicLabels keys, so the light-blue swatch is labelled exclusively 'إخفاء ميم ساكنة'. A user reading an Iqlab (إقلاب) letter and consulting the legend is told it is Ikhfa Meem Saakin — a genuinely different tajweed rule. The mapping/label mismatch is real and exactly as cited. The madd portion is weaker: madda_normal/permissible/obligatory (lines 56-58) collapse to ghunnah red whose label 'غنة / مد' (line 68) does at least name 'مد', so that part is grouping, not a false label — the claim slightly overstates it, but the core iqlab/ikhfa_shafawi conflation is solid. Bounded impact (only affects users who enable tajweed, open the legend, and know tajweed well enough to be misled; no crash/navigation breakage), so medium is the right severity, not high.

title: Tajweed colors are fixed RGB and not theme-aware (poor contrast on sepia/AMOLED)
description: TajweedColors are constant mid-tone values (e.g. silent #A0AEC0 light gray, ikhfaMeemSaakin #63B3ED light blue, idghamMeemSaakin #68D391 light green) used identically in every theme. On the sepia background (#FFFBEB) the light gray 'silent' and light green/blue meem colors have very low contrast; the same applies to legend swatches and rendered letters. No theme variant is provided.
impact: Silent-letter (gray) and meem-rule (pale blue/green) letters become hard to read in sepia and washed-out in light mode, and the legend swatches are nearly indistinguishable from the surface, hurting both readers and the legend's usefulness.
recommendation: Provide per-theme (or at least darker, higher-contrast) tajweed palettes, or darken the pale colors so they clear WCAG contrast against light/sepia surfaces.
evidence: static const Color silent = Color(0xFFA0AEC0); ... static const Color ikhfaMeemSaakin = Color(0xFF63B3ED);

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED (with one correction). The cited evidence is exact: theme_constants.dart:36-44 defines TajweedColors as fixed `static const Color` values (silent #A0AEC0, ikhfaMeemSaakin #63B3ED, idghamMeemSaakin #68D391, ikhfa #ED8936, etc.). These are applied raw with zero theme-awareness: tajweed_text.dart:61 does `final color = TajweedColors.colorMap[cssClass] ?? defaultColor;` and uses it directly as the verse-letter text color; tajweed_legend.dart:52,62 uses the raw color directly as the swatch fill. Neither widget branches on Theme/brightness, and no per-theme TajweedColors variant exists anywhere in the repo. I computed WCAG contrast: against the sepia background #FFFBEB, ikhfa=2.46, ikhfaMeem=2.20, silent=2.18, idghamMeem=1.79 — all below even the 3:1 large-text floor; ghunnah/idgham/qalqalah clear 3:1 large-text but fail normal 4.5:1. So the low-contrast-on-sepia claim is real and code-grounded.\n\nCORRECTION to the claim: it is NOT uniquely a sepia problem — the standard light/white theme produces nearly identical failing ratios (it's a light-surface defect sepia merely shares). More importantly, the claim's AMOLED assertion is WRONG: on pure black #000000 these pale colors have excellent contrast (9.2-11.3:1 for the meem/silent colors, 5.1+ for the rest). AMOLED is the best case, not a problem. Severity stays medium: it's a genuine accessibility/contrast flaw on light-family themes, but it is gated behind the opt-in showTajweed setting and the AMOLED half of the claim is false, so it does not warrant escalation.

title: Ayah marker uses ۝ combining mark, breaking marker rendering for multi-digit verses
description: formatAyahMarker in 'native' style returns '۝' + the Arabic-Indic digits ('۝' END OF AYAH). U+06DD is an enclosing combining mark designed to surround the digits that follow; rendering depends heavily on the font's support for sequence-enclosing. The verse card renders this with settings.quranFont (Hafs Smart / Amiri / etc.) at fontSize*0.62. For multi-digit verses (e.g. 255) many of these fonts do not enclose all digits, so the marker shows as a bare circle followed by digits rather than the expected end-of-ayah ornament.
impact: On surahs like Al-Baqarah, the end-of-ayah marker can render as a stray glyph plus loose numerals instead of the traditional enclosed ayah number, looking broken to readers expecting mushaf-style markers.
recommendation: Either use the 'badge' style (﴿..﴾) as default, or verify the chosen quranFont supports U+06DD enclosing of multi-digit sequences and fall back to a bracketed marker otherwise.
evidence: return '۝$num';

verdict.reasoning: Verified against source. lib/core/utils/arabic_utils.dart line 19 literally returns '۝$num' (U+06DD ARABIC END OF AYAH) for the 'native' style, matching the cited evidence and doc comment (line 12: ۝١). 'native' is genuinely the out-of-box default: SettingsState ctor (settings_provider.dart:42) and the datasource fallback (settings_local_datasource.dart:26) both default to 'native', and the settings UI presents it as 'قرآني' (reading_section.dart:144). Both call sites render the marker with settings.quranFont — verse_card.dart:48-49 at fontSize*0.62 and mushaf_view.dart:462-463 at fontSize*0.7 — exactly as described. U+06DD is a prefixed format control that is supposed to visually enclose the FOLLOWING digit sequence; this enclosure is heavily font-dependent. The app's registered font stack (pubspec: Amiri, Scheherazade New, Noto Naskh Arabic, Hafs Smart, Cairo) is mixed: Amiri/Hafs Smart enclose multi-digit ayah numbers correctly, but general-purpose fonts like Cairo and Noto Naskh Arabic typically do NOT enclose multi-digit sequences, so a verse like 255 renders as a bare circle followed by un-enclosed digits. Because quranFont is user-selectable across that mixed stack, the bug is genuine but conditional, not universal — which is why medium (not high) is the right severity. The RTL Directionality wrapper does not address this; it is purely a glyph/font-shaping issue. Location 14-20 is accurate.

title: Hardcoded amber Color(0xFFD97706) and Colors.amber instead of theme accent token

recommendation: Replace literal amber values with the appAccentColor token (or theme colorScheme.secondary/tertiary) so the accent stays consistent across themes.
evidence: color: const Color(0xFFD97706),  // _buildAyahMarkerStyle; and Colors.amber.withValues(alpha: 0.08)
