title: Word-by-word marker is detached onto its own line, unlike inline marker in other modes
description: In word-by-word mode the ayah marker is rendered as a separate right-aligned Text below the Wrap (with an 8px gap), whereas plain mode appends the marker inline after the last word and tajweed mode also places it on its own line but with 4px. The three modes present the end-of-ayah marker inconsistently (inline vs. block, 8px vs 4px spacing), and in WBW mode the floating marker reads as disconnected from the verse.
impact: Switching display modes shifts where/how the ayah number appears, creating a small but noticeable inconsistency; the detached WBW marker looks like an orphaned glyph rather than the verse terminator.
recommendation: Render the marker as a final inline item within the Wrap (an extra child) in WBW mode, and standardize the gap, so all three modes terminate the verse consistently.
evidence: const SizedBox(height: 8), Align(alignment: Alignment.centerRight, child: Text(marker, ...))

verdict.reasoning: The claim is factually accurate and code-grounded. In verse_card.dart _buildArabicText() there are three distinct, structurally inconsistent treatments of the end-of-ayah marker: (1) Word-by-word mode (lines 68-89) renders the marker as a separate widget below the WordByWordWidget — Column child = SizedBox(height: 8) then Align(centerRight, Text(marker)); (2) Tajweed mode (lines 96-116) also renders the marker on its own line but with only SizedBox(height: 4); (3) Plain mode (lines 120-146) appends the marker INLINE as TextSpan(text: ' $marker') right after the verse text. So the marker is inline in one mode and a detached block in the other two, and the two block modes even use different gaps (8 vs 4). All cited evidence (const SizedBox(height: 8), Align(alignment: Alignment.centerRight, child: Text(marker, ...))) matches the file exactly at the cited lines. The global RTL Directionality / forced 'ar' locale does not reconcile this: it only affects horizontal direction, not the structural inline-vs-separate-widget difference, and the inner WordByWordWidget re-wraps its children in its own RTL Directionality anyway. There is genuine (minor) user-visible impact: in WBW mode the marker floats on its own line disconnected from the last word. Severity 'low' is correct — it is a cosmetic/consistency polish issue, not a functional or accessibility defect. Note the recommendation to inline the marker into the Wrap is debatable (WBW word cells are two-row Columns, so a bare inline marker would not align cleanly), but that does not invalidate the underlying observation, which is real.

title: Time labels can squeeze controls off-screen on narrow phones / long durations
description: The controls Row places position/duration Text widgets with two Spacers around a center cluster (speed, repeat, play, stop). The Text widgets are unconstrained. A full-chapter recitation can exceed an hour, producing 'HH:MM:SS' (positionText/durationText switch to 8-char format in audio_provider _formatDuration line 74-76). With two such labels plus four controls on a Row in a narrow phone, the fixed-size IconButtons and labels have no Flexible/ellipsis, so a RenderFlex overflow is possible when the available width is tight.
impact: On long surahs (e.g. Al-Baqarah audio > 1h) or small screens, the bar can overflow with yellow/black stripes or clip the stop button.
recommendation: Wrap the time Text widgets in Flexible/FittedBox, or give them fixed minimum width with overflow handling, and reduce control spacing. Reserve width for the HH:MM:SS case explicitly.
evidence: Text(audioState.positionText ...) ... const Spacer() ... _SpeedButton ... _RepeatButton ... _PlayPauseButton ... IconButton(stop) ... const Spacer() ... Text(audioState.durationText ...)

verdict.reasoning: The code matches the claim exactly. In lib/features/reader/widgets/audio_player_bar.dart the Row (lines 56-104) places two unconstrained Text widgets (positionText line 59-66, durationText line 95-102) with two const Spacer()s (lines 68, 92) around a fixed-width center cluster: _SpeedButton (~40px), _RepeatButton (~30px+), _PlayPauseButton (40-48px IconButton), and a stop IconButton (default ~48px min tap target), separated by SizedBoxes. None of the time Text widgets are wrapped in Flexible/FittedBox or given overflow:ellipsis. I confirmed in audio_provider.dart lines 70-77 that _formatDuration switches to 8-char 'HH:MM:SS' when hours > 0, which is genuinely reachable (e.g. Al-Baqarah mujawwad recitations exceed an hour). Spacers collapse to 0 width under pressure, so they offer no protection: when fixed children + two labels + 24px horizontal padding exceed available width, a RenderFlex overflow results instead of graceful truncation. I also confirmed there is no global textScaler/textScaleFactor clamp anywhere in lib/, so accessibility font scaling enlarges both the 11px labels and the IconButtons, making overflow more likely. So the flaw is real and the cited location/evidence are correct. However, the realistic trigger is narrow: the minimum content width (~300-310px) still fits a standard 320dp phone at default text scale, and the hour-format only appears for the longest chapters. Overflow requires the combination of hour-plus audio AND a very narrow device or elevated text scale, and it never occurs in the common (sub-hour, default-scale) case. That low probability of real user impact warrants downgrading from medium to low. The recommendation (wrap time labels in Flexible/FittedBox, reserve HH:MM:SS width) is valid.

title: Audio bar offers no reciter selection or surah/verse identity
description: The persistent audio bar exposes seek, speed, repeat, play/pause and stop, but never shows WHAT is playing (no surah name / verse key from audioState.currentVerseKey or currentChapterId) and provides no way to change the reciter. selectedReciterId is only changeable deep in Settings (audio_section.dart). The bar reads like a generic media bar with no context.
impact: User listening cannot tell which verse/surah is playing from the bar, and cannot switch reciter without leaving the reader and digging into Settings. Confusing for the core listening use case.
recommendation: Add a label showing the current surah/verse (audioState.currentVerseKey) and a reciter quick-picker (PopupMenu like speed/repeat) that calls settings to change selectedReciterId and restarts playback.
evidence: final audioState = ref.watch(audioProvider); ... // Controls row ... no use of audioState.currentVerseKey / currentChapterId anywhere in the bar

verdict.reasoning:
The claim has two parts; only part of it survives scrutiny, and the severity is overstated.

PART 1 ("never shows WHAT is playing"): Literally true of AudioPlayerBar in isolation - lines 31-108 contain no reference to audioState.currentVerseKey or currentChapterId; the bar only shows progress slider, time/duration, speed, repeat, play/pause, stop. HOWEVER the UX framing is largely mitigated by surrounding context: (a) AudioPlayerBar is always rendered at the bottom of the reader screen (reader_screen.dart:516 and :552), whose AppBar title already displays the surah name chapter?.nameArabic (reader_screen.dart:347-349); (b) the currently-playing verse is visually highlighted in the verse list via isCurrentVerse/isPlayingAudio (reader_screen.dart:464-501); and (c) the app's persistent shell mini-player DOES show identity text - 'الآية {currentVerseKey}' / 'سورة {currentChapterId}' (app_shell.dart:113-115). So the user is not actually left guessing what's playing; the missing in-bar label is a minor polish gap, not high-severity confusion.

PART 2 ("no way to change reciter; only deep in Settings"): Verifiably correct. The bar has Speed (_SpeedButton, lines 71/149-197) and Repeat (_RepeatButton, lines 75/199-264) PopupMenus but NO reciter picker. selectedReciterId is mutated only via settings (settings_provider.dart:205) surfaced through audio_section.dart -> reciter_selector_sheet.dart, reachable only from the Settings tab. There is no reciter quick-switch anywhere in the reader. This is a genuine, real UX friction point.

Conclusion: the flaw is real (reciter quick-pick is genuinely absent; in-bar identity label is genuinely absent) but overstated as high. The audioProvider exposes currentVerseKey/currentChapterId (audio_provider.dart:14-15) so adding a label is trivial, and reciter change requires leaving the reader entirely - a real discoverability/convenience gap, but not blocking or confusing since surah context and now-playing verse are already on screen. Medium severity is appropriate.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/features/reader/widgets/audio_player_bar.dart:54-105 (controls row where identity label and reciter picker would belong)

title: Slider is interactive while audio is still loading (duration unknown)
description: The Slider is always enabled. While isLoading is true the duration is Duration.zero, so progress is 0.0 (audio_provider line 65-68) and seekToPercent computes targetMs from a zero duration (line 260), making any drag a no-op that snaps back. The slider gives false affordance during loading/buffering.
impact: User drags the progress bar during buffering and nothing happens; thumb jumps back to 0. Feels broken.
recommendation: Disable the Slider (onChanged: null) or show an indeterminate/loading track when audioState.isLoading or duration == Duration.zero.
evidence: Slider(value: audioState.progress, onChanged: (value) { ref.read(audioProvider.notifier).seekToPercent(value); })

verdict.reasoning: The claim is code-accurate. In lib/features/reader/widgets/audio_player_bar.dart lines 45-51 the Slider has an always-non-null onChanged (no isLoading/duration guard) and no min/max override (defaults 0.0-1.0), so it is always interactive. In lib/features/reader/providers/audio_provider.dart, progress (lines 65-68) returns 0.0 when duration.inMilliseconds == 0 (the case during loading/buffering before durationStream emits, since duration defaults to Duration.zero at line 29). seekToPercent (lines 259-262) computes targetMs = duration.inMilliseconds * percent, which is 0 for any percent when duration is zero, so seek(Duration.zero) is a no-op that snaps the thumb back to 0. So the slider does present false affordance during loading. Nothing in the RTL/Directionality/theme wrapper changes this, and the cited line numbers are correct. However, severity is overstated as medium. Impact is minor polish: the loading window is brief (single network fetch + buffer), the play/pause control already swaps to a CircularProgressIndicator during isLoading (lines 120-132) giving a clear loading signal, and dragging during loading merely snaps to 0 which is already where the thumb sits. No crash, stuck state, or data loss. This is a low-severity affordance nit, not a medium-severity defect.

title: ShareSheet opened without isScrollControlled, clipping content on small screens
description: _showShareSheet calls showModalBottomSheet WITHOUT isScrollControlled: true (unlike _showTafsirSheet and _showNoteSheet which set it). The ShareSheet itself sets maxHeightFraction: 0.6 but a default modal bottom sheet is capped at ~9/16 of screen height and never grows; a long verse preview (verse.textUthmani at fontSize 18, height 2.0) plus two button rows can exceed that cap with no scroll, causing a bottom overflow.
impact: For long verses the share preview/buttons overflow or get clipped at the bottom of the sheet; the native share button may be unreachable.
recommendation: Add isScrollControlled: true to _showShareSheet to match the other sheets, and/or make ShareSheet content scrollable.
evidence: void _showShareSheet(...) { showModalBottomSheet(context: context, useSafeArea: true, backgroundColor: Colors.transparent, builder: (_) => ShareSheet(...)); }  // no isScrollControlled

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed. reader_screen.dart:295-301 (_showShareSheet) calls showModalBottomSheet WITHOUT isScrollControlled:true, while the sibling _showTafsirSheet (line 256) and _showNoteSheet (line 269) both set it. The overflow mechanism is real and verified: ShareSheet (share_sheet.dart) uses BaseBottomSheet with maxHeightFraction:0.6; BaseBottomSheet (base_bottom_sheet.dart:86) puts content in Flexible(child: child) — NOT a scroll view — and ShareSheet's child is a non-scrollable Column(mainAxisSize:MainAxisSize.min) containing a verse preview (verse.textUthmani at fontSize 18, height 2.0, lines 49-59), a reference, two button rows, and a FilledButton. I grep-confirmed there is no SingleChildScrollView/ListView in ShareSheet (only two horizontal Expanded button wrappers). Without isScrollControlled the modal is capped at the framework default (~9/16 of available height), which is tighter than the 0.6 fraction; on the longest verses (e.g. 2:282) the intrinsic Column height exceeds the cap and, being non-scrollable, produces a RenderFlex bottom overflow / clipped share button on smaller screens. The contrast with TafsirSheet is instructive: TafsirSheet survives because it wraps content in Flexible(SingleChildScrollView) (tafsir_sheet.dart:145-146), not merely because of isScrollControlled. Severity lowered from high to medium: the defect is conditional (only longest verses on smaller devices) and is visual clipping, not data loss or a crash. Note: the claim's suggested fix of adding isScrollControlled alone is necessary but not fully sufficient — making ShareSheet's content scrollable (as TafsirSheet does) is the complete fix — but the cited flaw itself is genuine and code-grounded.

title: Page numbers and verse counts shown in Western digits inside Arabic text
description: The surah index subtitle interpolates raw ints: 'صفحة $startPage - عدد الآيات ${chapter.versesCount} ...'. toArabicNumeral is imported and used for the chapter number circle (line 255) but NOT for the page number or verse count, so an all-Arabic line mixes ASCII digits (e.g. 'صفحة 50 - عدد الآيات 286') breaking RTL digit consistency used elsewhere in the app.
impact: Inconsistent numerals within Arabic UI; numbers may render in the wrong visual order/style versus the rest of the app which uses Arabic-Indic digits.
recommendation: Wrap startPage and chapter.versesCount with toArabicNumeral(...) like the chapter number is.
evidence: 'صفحة $startPage - عدد الآيات ${chapter.versesCount} - ${chapter.revelationPlace == "makkah" ? "مكية" : "مدنية"}'

The same widget uses toArabicNumeral(chapter.id) at line 255 for the chapter number circle, proving the function is imported (line 6) and intentionally applied for digit consistency right beside this subtitle. toArabicNumeral (lib/core/utils/arabic_utils.dart) is the app-wide convention, used across 18 files. Flutter's Directionality/RTL wrapper only affects layout order, not glyph substitution — ASCII 0-9 render as Western digits regardless of textDirection, and there is no Flutter theme/locale mechanism that auto-converts them. So the inconsistency genuinely renders. The flaw is real, code-grounded, and user-visible. Severity medium is reasonable (a clear deviation from the codebase's own numeral standard), though it sits at the lower edge of medium since it is a cosmetic inconsistency in a secondary navigation index sheet.

title: Tafsir verse text uses settings.quranFont but tafsir body hardcodes 'Amiri'
description: The verse preview respects the user's chosen quran font (line 162 fontFamily: settings.quranFont) but the tafsir body text hardcodes fontFamily: 'Amiri' (line 186), ignoring the user's font/script preference for the explanatory Arabic text.

title: Note sheet has no cancel/close affordance and silently no-ops on empty save

title: Double bottom-sheet container nesting (rounded corners + background drawn twice) in NoteSheet

verdict.reasoning: Verified against both files. Net: structurally real but cosmetic/no observable user-facing defect, so severity low is correct.

title: Tafsir in-sheet search highlight uses case-insensitive ASCII match unsuited to Arabic
description: _highlightedTextSpan matches via text.toLowerCase()/query.toLowerCase() and substring indices. impact: In-sheet tafsir search appears to not find obviously-present words because diacritics/alef variants aren't normalized; feature feels broken for Arabic.
recommendation: Normalize both query and text (strip tashkeel, unify alef/hamza/ta-marbuta) before indexOf matching.
evidence: final lcText = text.toLowerCase(); final lcQuery = query.toLowerCase(); ... final idx = lcText.indexOf(lcQuery, start);

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed at lib/features/reader/widgets/tafsir_sheet.dart:48-78. _highlightedTextSpan does lcText = text.toLowerCase(), lcQuery = query.toLowerCase() (lines 51-52) then lcText.indexOf(lcQuery) (line 57). toLowerCase() is a no-op for Arabic, and there is NO diacritic/orthographic normalization anywhere: a codebase-wide grep for normaliz/tashkeel/harakat/alef/hamza/\u064x returned zero matches, and arabic_utils.dart only contains numeral/time/reference helpers. All four tafsir options (السعدي, الميسر, ابن كثير, البغوي in quran_constants.dart:49-54) are Arabic-language sources whose published text commonly carries tashkeel. So a user typing a word without harakat against tafsir text that contains harakat yields indexOf == -1 and no highlight. The flaw is genuine. Two caveats keep it at 'low': (1) this is an in-sheet find/highlight convenience over already-displayed text — failure only means the amber highlight does not appear; nothing crashes and no data is lost; (2) the description's 'misses most real matches' is overstated, since some sources (e.g. Al-Muyassar id 16) are stored with little/no tashkeel and match fine. Severity 'low' is appropriate as rated. Cited location 48-78 is exact.

title: Khatmah plans are exported but never restored on import (silent data loss)

// _importData: only bookmarks and notes loops; no khatmahPlans handling

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly. In lib/features/settings/widgets/backup_section.dart, _exportData writes a 'khatmahPlans' array (lines 83-90: progressState.khatmahPlans.map(...).toList()). _importData (lines 110-162) only reads data['bookmarks'] (lines 134-139, via bookmarkNotifier.importBookmark) and data['notes'] (lines 142-146, via importNote). A whole-lib grep confirms there is NO importKhatmah/importPlan/import path of any kind: progress_provider.dart's ProgressNotifier has no import method (and in fact no add/save khatmah method at all here); saveKhatmahPlans exists only in progress_local_datasource.dart (line 135) and is called solely from khatmah_screen.dart during normal use, never from import. Severity adjusted from critical to high: this is genuine silent data loss, but khatmah plans are lightweight regenerable metadata (name, totalDays, startDate, completedDays, currentDay) rather than irreplaceable user-authored content, the backup file itself is not corrupted, and a plan can be recreated quickly — so impact is real but below critical.

Every verse's Wrap then masks words via the SAME flat set: `_hiddenWordIndices.contains(wi)` (line 257). At thematic_screen.dart:55-64 the topic card's onTap calls Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => _ThematicVersesScreen(...))), while the verse tap inside that detail screen (line 212) uses context.pushNamed('reader', ...). When the verse tap then fires context.pushNamed('reader') (reader declares parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey), GoRouter pushes onto the root navigator on top of an imperatively-pushed route it does not track, leaving GoRouter's route stack/URL state out of sync with the actual Navigator stack — a latent back-handling/pop-semantics hazard. However, the concrete breakage is limited: it is a leaf detail screen with no deep-link entry point, the reader push still functionally lands on top, and ordinary system/AppBar back pops the MaterialPageRoute normally, so no guaranteed crash or visible-in-normal-use failure occurs. title: Division by zero risk when totalVerses is 0 in recent-readings progress

There is no guard.

final percent = (progress.versesRead / progress.totalVerses * 100).round();
... value: progress.versesRead / progress.totalVerses,

verdict.reasoning:
The cited code is accurate. stats_screen.dart:144 does `(progress.versesRead / progress.totalVerses * 100).round()` and line 187 sets LinearProgressIndicator `value: progress.versesRead / progress.totalVerses`, with no guard against a zero divisor. The crash mechanism is also technically correct: in Dart int `/` returns a double, so n/0 yields Infinity (0/0 yields NaN), `.round()` on Infinity/NaN throws UnsupportedError, and LinearProgressIndicator rejects non-finite values. Notably the entity ReadingProgress already exposes a SAFE getter `progressPercent => totalVerses > 0 ? ... : 0.0` (reading_progress.dart:18-19), which the stats screen ignores in favor of raw inline division — so this is a genuine defensive-coding gap and an inconsistency with the codebase's own guarded helper.

HOWEVER, the trigger condition (totalVerses == 0) is unreachable in normal operation. The `readingProgress` SharedPreferences key is written ONLY by saveProgress() <- updateProgress() (progress_provider.dart:55-103), which is fed exclusively from reader_screen.dart. Every call site supplies totalVerses from real chapter data: `_totalVersesForChapter` returns `chapter?.versesCount ?? 286` (line 106), and other call sites use `chapter?.versesCount ?? verses.length` inside non-empty-verses branches. Real Quran chapters have a minimum of 3 verses, so versesCount is never 0, and all fallbacks (286, verses.length) are non-zero. The backup/import feature (backup_section.dart) does NOT import reading progress at all (only bookmarks, notes, khatmah plans), so there is no untrusted-input path. The only way to hit totalVerses==0 is externally corrupted/hand-edited persisted JSON, which getProgress() casts without validation (progress_local_datasource.dart:29).

So: real latent bug and worth a one-line guard (especially since a safe getter already exists), but essentially zero real-world user impact. Medium severity overstates it; low is appropriate.

impact: Slightly reduced legibility of the headline percentage on certain themes for low-vision users; the most prominent number on the dashboard does not adapt.
recommendation: Use theme.colorScheme.primary (or appAccentColor) and verify contrast across all four themes.
evidence: Text('${(overallProgress * 100).toStringAsFixed(1)}%', style: TextStyle(fontSize: 28, ... color: Colors.amber[700]))

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed at the exact cited lines. Line 56: `color: Colors.amber[700]` on the 28sp bold overall-progress percentage; line 201: `color: percent >= 100 ? Colors.green : Colors.amber[700]` on the per-row percent text. Both hardcode Colors.amber[700] (#FFA000) regardless of theme. title: Recent readings re-resolves chaptersAsync per-row and silently drops rows while loading

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed in lib/features/stats/screens/stats_screen.dart. Inside the else-branch (lines 137-216), topEntries.map((entry){...}) iterates up to 10 progress rows, and EACH row returns chaptersAsync.whenOrNull(data: (chapters){...}) ?? const SizedBox.shrink() (lines 146-214). Riverpod's whenOrNull only handles the data case; during loading or error it returns null, so the ?? collapses every row to SizedBox.shrink(). chaptersProvider (chapters_provider.dart:40-43) is a real async FutureProvider calling repository.getChapters() (network/DB), so a loading window genuinely exists, especially on cold start. The section header 'آخر القراءات' (lines 118-121) and its SizedBox(height:12) are rendered unconditionally outside the whenOrNull, so while chapters load the header sits above empty space with no spinner/placeholder. 'سورة N'), but it only applies once data is available and does not cover loading/error, so the claim's core point stands. title: Mini audio player is not tappable to reopen the reader

title: No SystemUiOverlayStyle / status bar styling anywhere in the app
description: MaterialApp.router sets themes but never configures the system status bar / navigation bar appearance. A grep for SystemUiOverlayStyle, setSystemUIOverlayStyle and AnnotatedRegion across the whole lib/ returns zero matches. The AppBarTheme does not set systemOverlayStyle either. With the AMOLED (pure black #000000) and dark themes, the status bar icons are not forced to light, and with light/sepia themes they are not forced to dark, so on many OEM ROMs the status bar icons can be unreadable (e.g. light icons on the light sepia background, or dark icons on AMOLED black).
impact: Status bar clock/battery icons can become invisible or low-contrast depending on theme and device default, especially on AMOLED black and light sepia. Also the Android navigation bar color is left at the system default and will not match the themed bottom NavigationBar.
recommendation: Set systemOverlayStyle per theme in AppBarTheme (or wrap with AnnotatedRegion<SystemUiOverlayStyle> in app.dart) — light themes -> SystemUiOverlayStyle.dark, dark/amoled -> SystemUiOverlayStyle.light — and set systemNavigationBarColor to match the NavigationBar surface.
evidence: Grep for 'SystemUiOverlayStyle|setSystemUIOverlayStyle|AnnotatedRegion' across lib/ -> 'No files found'. AppBarTheme(...) blocks in app_theme.dart set elevation/backgroundColor but never systemOverlayStyle.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual core of the claim is verified. Grep across lib/ confirms zero matches for SystemUiOverlayStyle, setSystemUIOverlayStyle, AnnotatedRegion, or systemOverlayStyle; the only SystemChrome use is setPreferredOrientations in main.dart:15. lib/app.dart (lines 41-62) builds MaterialApp.router with themes but never configures system overlay styling, and the builder only wraps in Directionality. All four AppBarTheme blocks in lib/core/theme/app_theme.dart (light L12, dark L60, sepia L118, amoled L193) set centerTitle/elevation/background/foreground but never systemOverlayStyle. So the app never explicitly controls the status/navigation bar. The cited location is correct.

However, the claim OVERSTATES the status-bar impact. Flutter's AppBar widget has a built-in fallback: when systemOverlayStyle is null in both the widget and AppBarTheme, AppBar derives a default from the estimated brightness of its background color (ThemeData.estimateBrightnessForColor). Since each AppBarTheme uses the theme's surface/background color, status-bar icon brightness IS auto-contrasted on every AppBar-equipped screen while that AppBar is mounted. The specific failures the claim predicts ("dark icons on AMOLED black", "light icons on sepia") would largely NOT occur on AppBar screens because Flutter auto-flips them. The genuine residual gaps are: (1) the system NAVIGATION bar color/icon contrast is never set, so on edge-to-edge Android it stays at the platform default and won't match the dark/AMOLED/sepia NavigationBar surface in app_shell.dart; (2) AppBar-less surfaces such as the mushaf PageView reader inherit whatever overlay style the previous AppBar left, which can be stale/wrong. These are real polish/consistency defects worth fixing via systemOverlayStyle per theme plus systemNavigationBarColor, but they do not make the status bar "unreadable across many screens." Real flaw, mis-rated; downgrade high -> medium.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/app.dart:41-62 (and lib/core/theme/app_theme.dart AppBarTheme blocks at lines 12, 60, 118, 193)

recommendation: Replace the four literals with theme.colorScheme.primary (or import appAccentColor and the amoled variant via the active theme). Since the widget already receives `theme`, use theme.colorScheme.primary.
evidence: valueColor: const AlwaysStoppedAnimation(Color(0xFFD97706)) ... Icon(Icons.music_note, ..., color: Color(0xFFD97706)) ... CircularProgressIndicator(strokeWidth: 2, color: Color(0xFFD97706)) ... color: const Color(0xFFD97706)

title: Only 3 of 10 screens reachable from bottom nav; 7 buried behind a Home-only popup
description: The ShellRoute (with the bottom NavigationBar) hosts only home, bookmarks, settings. The other 7 routes — '/reader/:chapterId', '/notes', '/juz', '/khatmah', '/memorization', '/stats', '/thematic' — are all GoRoutes with parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey, so they render full-screen with no bottom nav. app_shell.dart:34-62 confirms the NavigationBar has exactly 3 destinations (home/bookmarks/settings) and no 'More' tab or drawer. title: Mini player shows raw Latin chapter id and bare verse key, not Arabic numerals/name

Here a chapter is shown as a Western digit with no surah name, and the verse key as 'chapter:verse' Latin form. In an RTL all-Arabic UI this looks unlocalized, and a bare '18' with no name is uninformative.

recommendation: Resolve the chapter name (from chaptersProvider) and pass through toArabicNumeral() for any digits, e.g. 'سورة الكهف' or 'الآية ٢٥٥'. Avoid showing the raw '2:255' verse key.

""}'. In lib/features/reader/providers/audio_provider.dart, currentVerseKey is a String holding the raw Quran.com key (e.g. "2:255", set in playVerse line 208) and currentChapterId is a bare int (e.g. 18, set in playChapter). Refutation attempts failed: the RTL Directionality wrapper does not transliterate digits, and there is no default that substitutes the surah name. title: main() does no error handling around DB init; a failed initialize blocks app launch
description: main awaits initializer.initializeIfNeeded() and localDataSource.initialize() before runApp, with no try/catch and no error UI. If the bundled-JSON population or DB open throws (corrupt DB, disk full, integrity-check failure per the transaction-wrapped init noted in CLAUDE.md), the exception propagates out of main and runApp is never reached, so the user sees a blank/crashed app with no message or retry.
impact: Any first-launch DB initialization failure results in a hard, silent crash with no recovery path or user-facing error, instead of degrading to API/online mode or showing a retry screen.
recommendation: Wrap the initialization in try/catch; on failure still runApp with a minimal error/retry screen (or proceed in online-only mode) and log via AppLogger. Consider runZonedGuarded + FlutterError.onError for global crash capture.
evidence: final initializer = DatabaseInitializer(db); await initializer.initializeIfNeeded(); final localDataSource = QuranLocalDataSource(db: db); await localDataSource.initialize(); runApp(...) // no try/catch, no error fallback

verdict.reasoning: Verified in lib/main.dart (lines 11-40): main() awaits database init then calls runApp with no try/catch and no global error handler. Confirmed no runZonedGuarded, FlutterError.onError, or ErrorWidget.builder anywhere in lib/. The throw path is real: initializer.initializeIfNeeded() (lib/core/database/database_initializer.dart:14) calls _db.isPopulated() unguarded (app_database.dart:159-165 runs a getSingle() query with no try/catch — throws if the SQLite DB fails to open/query), and on first launch calls _populateFromBundle() (line 27) directly with no try/catch around rootBundle.loadString, jsonDecode, the transaction, or rebuildFtsIndex. Any of these throwing propagates out of main(), so runApp is never reached and the user gets a blank/crashed app with no message or retry. One correction to the claim's evidence: it also cites localDataSource.initialize() as a throw path, but that method (quran_local_datasource.dart:27-56) wraps everything in try/catch and swallows exceptions (sets _jsonInitialized=false and returns), so it cannot throw out of main. The flaw stands regardless because initializeIfNeeded() can throw. Medium severity is correct: failure modes (corrupt DB, disk full, missing/corrupt asset, integrity re-population failure) are uncommon and don't affect the happy path, but when they occur the user is hard-locked out of the app with zero feedback or recovery.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/main.dart:11-40 (throw path: lib/core/database/database_initializer.dart:14-28 via _db.isPopulated() at lib/core/database/app_database.dart:159; localDataSource.initialize() is NOT a throw path)

title: Secondary screens pushed on root navigator lose bottom nav AND mini audio player with no alternative nav
description: Notes, Juz, Khatmah, Memorization, Stats, and Thematic are all GoRoutes with parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey, so they render OUTSIDE the ShellRoute. The AppShell (bottom NavigationBar + mini audio player) only wraps '/', '/bookmarks', '/settings'. Consequently every secondary screen has no bottom tab bar and no persistent mini-player. If audio is playing and the user opens e.g. the Juz index, the mini-player controls vanish entirely, leaving no way to pause/stop without going back. The only navigation off these screens is the AppBar back button.
impact: Users lose tab-level navigation and lose all audio playback controls on 6 screens. Playing audio then opening any tool means audio keeps playing with no visible control. Inconsistent chrome between primary and secondary screens is disorienting.
recommendation: Either move these routes inside the ShellRoute (so they keep the shell chrome), or render the mini audio player at the app level (above the Navigator) so playback controls persist on every screen.
evidence: GoRoute(path: '/juz', name: RouteNames.juz, parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey, builder: (context, state) => const JuzNavigatorScreen())  // outside ShellRoute => no AppShell, no _MiniAudioPlayer

verdict.reasoning: Verified factually. In lib/core/router/app_router.dart lines 67-102, the routes /notes, /juz, /khatmah, /memorization, /stats, /thematic are all GoRoute entries with parentNavigatorKey: _rootNavigatorKey, placed OUTSIDE the ShellRoute (lines 23-49). The ShellRoute's builder (AppShell) is the ONLY host of both the NavigationBar and the _MiniAudioPlayer (lib/core/widgets/app_shell.dart lines 25-66; mini-player rendered at lines 31-32 gated by audioState.hasAudio). AppShell wraps only '/', '/bookmarks', '/settings'. So all six secondary screens render with no bottom nav and no persistent mini-player. The 'maybe a wrapper handles it' defense fails: app.dart (lines 55-60) only adds an RTL Directionality wrapper and explicitly does NOT add any app-level audio player. The reader's own controls (AudioPlayerBar) are reader-screen-only and not present on these screens. The user-impact is concrete and verifiable: the mini-player exists specifically to give persistent playback controls, and it disappears on these routes. Stronger than claimed — the memorization screen (itself a no-shell root route) can START audio via ref.read(audioProvider.notifier).playVerse(...) at memorization_screen.dart line 223, yet offers no persistent play/pause/stop control; its only stop is a side effect of the 'رجوع' back button (line 169), so playback can be orphaned with no in-app global control. Severity stays high because orphaned, uncontrollable playback is trivially reachable; the only mild over-statement is the navigation portion (an AppBar back button does exist on each screen), which is why this isn't critical.
verdict.correctedLocation: lib/core/router/app_router.dart:67-102 (and lib/core/widgets/app_shell.dart:25-66 where the shell-only mini-player lives)

title: Tab switching destroys Home state (search query, scroll position) because tabs use go + NoTransitionPage with no state retention
description: The bottom nav calls context.goNamed for each tab and the ShellRoute swaps the single `child`. There is no StatefulShellRoute / IndexedStack, so HomeScreen (a ConsumerStatefulWidget holding _searchController and _submittedQuery) is disposed when the user switches to Bookmarks and recreated when returning. A user who searches, scrolls down the 114-chapter list, then peeks at Bookmarks loses their search results and scroll position on return.
impact: Scroll position and in-progress search are lost every time the user changes tabs and comes back. Feels like the app 'forgets' where they were.
recommendation: Use GoRouter's StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack so each tab branch keeps its own Navigator and state, preserving scroll/search across tab switches.
evidence: onDestinationSelected: (index) { switch (index) { case 0: context.goNamed(RouteNames.home); case 1: context.goNamed(RouteNames.bookmarks); ... } }  // single ShellRoute child, no IndexedStack

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual code. lib/core/router/app_router.dart line 23 uses a plain ShellRoute (not StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack) whose builder swaps a single `child` (line 25), and each tab is a separate GoRoute returning a NoTransitionPage (lines 30-32, 37-39, 44-46). lib/core/widgets/app_shell.dart lines 36-44 calls context.goNamed for each tab exactly as the evidence cites — the cited location is accurate. HomeScreen is a ConsumerStatefulWidget (home_screen.dart line 16) whose state lives entirely in _HomeScreenState: _searchController (line 24), _submittedQuery (line 25), and the CustomScrollView scroll offset (line 112). With a single-child ShellRoute, going to /bookmarks removes the Home route from the shell Navigator, so its element unmounts and dispose() runs (line 35), destroying _searchController and _submittedQuery; returning rebuilds a fresh empty Home with the list scrolled to top. I confirmed via grep that the codebase contains no PageStorageKey, AutomaticKeepAlive, keepAlive, IndexedStack, or StatefulShellRoute anywhere, so nothing mitigates this. Note: chaptersProvider/quranSearchProvider are Riverpod-cached, so fetched data does not re-download — but the lost items are UI state (typed query, submitted-search view, scroll position), which is exactly what the claim describes. This is the well-known reason StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack exists; the recommended fix is correct. Real, reproducible UX regression on a primary flow but no crash/data loss, so medium severity stands.

title: Thematic verse list sub-screen uses raw Navigator.push(MaterialPageRoute) instead of GoRouter
description: Tapping a thematic topic opens _ThematicVersesScreen via Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(...)), bypassing GoRouter entirely. Every other navigation in the app goes through GoRouter (go/push/pushNamed). This sub-screen is not a registered route, has no URL, cannot be deep-linked, and is invisible to GoRouter redirect/restoration logic. It mixes two navigation systems on the root navigator.
impact: Inconsistent navigation stack management; the thematic detail screen cannot be deep-linked or restored, and mixing imperative Navigator with declarative GoRouter risks back-stack inconsistencies.
recommendation: Register _ThematicVersesScreen as a GoRoute (e.g. /thematic/:topic) and navigate via context.pushNamed, or pass the topic as an extra, for consistency with the rest of the app.
evidence: Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => _ThematicVersesScreen(topicName: topic.name, ...)))

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed at lib/features/thematic/screens/thematic_screen.dart:55-65. The topic-card onTap calls Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => _ThematicVersesScreen(...))), exactly as the evidence cites. A repo-wide Grep for Navigator.push(MaterialPageRoute) returns this as the ONLY occurrence in lib/ — every other screen is registered as a GoRoute in lib/core/router/app_router.dart (home, bookmarks, settings, reader, notes, juz, khatmah, memorization, stats, thematic) and navigated via go/push/pushNamed. The inconsistency is especially clear because the same file at line 212 navigates to the reader via context.pushNamed('reader', ...) — GoRouter — so it mixes both systems within one file. _ThematicVersesScreen is a private widget with no GoRoute, no path, and no name: it cannot be deep-linked and is invisible to GoRouter's URL/redirect/restoration model. The project explicitly adopted route_names.dart constants and a centralized router as an architectural standard (per CLAUDE.md item 32), making this the lone documented violation. The claim is real and the location is accurate. Severity 'medium' is reasonable: behavior still works (pushed on the root navigator, same surface GoRouter would use, back navigation functions), so the impact is primarily consistency/maintainability plus loss of deep-linkability rather than a user-facing breakage. It sits at the low end of medium but does not warrant downgrade given it violates the codebase's stated navigation standard.

title: Verse references displayed with Latin digits while rest of UI uses Arabic-Indic
description: The list subtitle renders the raw verseKey (e.g. '2:255') with Western/Latin digits, while the title directly above on the same tile uses toArabicNumeral to show 'سورة ٢ - الآية ٢٥٥'. The dedicated helper formatVerseReference() in lib/core/utils/arabic_utils.dart (which would localize the key to Arabic-Indic) exists but is never used anywhere. Same raw-key display appears in bookmarks (line 139), notes (line 81), and juz_navigator (line 63).
impact: Same screen shows two number systems side by side (Arabic-Indic ٢٥٥ in the title, Latin 2:255 in the subtitle), which looks inconsistent and unpolished to Arabic readers and undermines the fully-Arabic experience.
recommendation: Display references through formatVerseReference() / toArabicNumeral so the colon-separated key is shown in Arabic-Indic numerals (e.g. ٢:٢٥٥), consistently across thematic, bookmarks, notes, and juz_navigator.
evidence:
title: Text('سورة ${toArabicNumeral(chapterId)} - الآية ...')
...
subtitle: Text(
  verseKey,   // raw '2:255' Latin digits

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed in code. In lib/features/thematic/screens/thematic_screen.dart the ListTile title (line 192) builds 'سورة ${toArabicNumeral(chapterId)} - الآية ${toArabicNumeral(...)}' (Arabic-Indic digits), while the subtitle directly below (lines 200-201) renders the raw verseKey via Text(verseKey) — so '2:255' shows with Latin glyphs on the very same tile. The RTL Directionality wrapper in app.dart only affects text direction/ordering, NOT digit glyph substitution; Latin digits stay Latin unless toArabicNumeral is applied, which it is not here. Grep confirms formatVerseReference() in lib/core/utils/arabic_utils.dart (line 23) is defined but never called anywhere. The companion claims also check out: bookmarks_screen.dart line 139 ('${bookmark.chapterName} • ${bookmark.verseKey}'), notes_screen.dart line 81 (same pattern), and juz_navigator_screen.dart line 63 (Text(juz.verseKey)) all emit the raw colon-separated key with Latin digits in an app that is forced to Arabic/RTL and uses toArabicNumeral elsewhere. So the flaw genuinely exists and the cited evidence is accurate. I downgrade severity from high to medium: the affected text is a de-emphasized secondary subtitle (alpha 0.4), and in bookmarks/notes it is preceded by the localized Arabic chapter name, so it is a cosmetic localization/consistency inconsistency rather than broken functionality, unreadable content, or a navigation/data defect.

title: Page-jump dialog mixes Arabic-Indic hint with Latin suffix and forces LTR field
description: The page-jump TextField sets hintText: '١ - ٦٠٤' (Arabic-Indic) but suffixText: '/ 604' (Latin), and forces textDirection: TextDirection.ltr. So the same input row shows the page range in two different numeral systems, and the typed value will be Latin while the surrounding app is Arabic-Indic. The page indicator that triggers this dialog (line 223) shows the current page in Arabic-Indic via toArabicNumeral, so the dialog contradicts it.
impact: User taps an Arabic-Indic page number (e.g. ٢٥٠), opens the dialog and sees a Latin '/ 604' counter plus an Arabic-Indic hint, creating a jarring mixed-numeral, mixed-direction prompt.
recommendation: Make the suffix Arabic-Indic ('/ ٦٠٤') to match the hint and the indicator, or make both Latin consistently. Parsing already uses int.tryParse so input localization can be handled, but at minimum align the displayed numerals.
evidence:
hintText: '١ - ٦٠٤',
suffixText: '/ 604',
...
textDirection: TextDirection.ltr,

verdict.reasoning: The cited code is accurate. In mushaf_view.dart line 70 the field's hintText is '١ - ٦٠٤' (Arabic-Indic, ٦٠٤=604) while line 71's suffixText is '/ 604' (Latin), so the same maximum-page number appears in two different numeral systems on one input row — a genuine typographic inconsistency, not speculation. The dialog is launched from the page indicator at line 208-223, which renders the current page via toArabicNumeral (confirmed in arabic_utils.dart lines 2-8 to produce Arabic-Indic digits), so the dialog's Latin suffix does contradict the Arabic-Indic indicator and hint. This is real and code-grounded. However, the claim overstates two things: (1) textDirection: TextDirection.ltr (line 68) is a defensible idiom for a numeric field inside a globally RTL app and is not itself a defect; and (2) functionality is unaffected — int.tryParse handles input and the app forces locale 'ar', so an Arabic numeric keyboard's digits still parse. Net user impact is a minor cosmetic mixed-numeral inconsistency in one rarely-seen dialog, which warrants 'low' rather than 'medium'.

title: ChoiceChip and summary mix Latin digits with Arabic words
description: The khatmah-duration chips build labels as '$days يوم' where days is an int (7, 14, 30, 60), producing '7 يوم' with Latin digits inline with the Arabic word. The summary line '${(6236 / selectedDays).ceil()} آية يوميًا' likewise injects a Latin number into an Arabic sentence. The app otherwise renders counts via toArabicNumeral.
impact: Arabic users see '7 يوم' / '208 آية يوميًا' instead of '٧ يوم' / '٢٠٨ آية يوميًا', an inconsistent and non-native presentation in a primary planning dialog.
recommendation: Wrap the numbers in toArabicNumeral, e.g. Text('${toArabicNumeral(days)} يوم') and 'حوالي ${toArabicNumeral((6236 / selectedDays).ceil())} آية يوميًا'.
evidence:
label: Text('$days يوم'),
...
'حوالي ${(6236 / selectedDays).ceil()} آية يوميًا',

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the actual file. Line 44 builds the ChoiceChip label as Text('$days يوم') where days is a raw int (7, 14, 30, 60), and line 58 builds 'حوالي ${(6236 / selectedDays).ceil()} آية يوميًا' interpolating a raw int. Both render Western/Latin digits (e.g. "7 يوم", "208 آية يوميًا") inline with Arabic words. This is a real inconsistency, not opinion: the SAME file uses toArabicNumeral everywhere else — line 276 ('${toArabicNumeral(plan.currentDay)} / ${toArabicNumeral(plan.totalDays)} يوم'), line 285, and line 369 — and the helper is already imported on line 5. The app's RTL Directionality wrapper does NOT fix this; RTL only controls layout direction, not the actual Unicode digit glyphs, so Latin digits still render as 7/14/30. The flaw is genuine but purely cosmetic (digit glyph style in a creation dialog, no functional/data impact), so medium is slightly overstated; low is the accurate severity. The recommendation (wrap in toArabicNumeral) is correct.

title: Translation text right-aligned without textDirection (fails if translation is LTR)
description: The translation Text uses textAlign: TextAlign.right but sets no textDirection, so it inherits the global RTL. Translation strings are user-selectable and can be non-Arabic (English etc.). For an LTR translation, TextAlign.right hard-pins it to the right edge and RTL inheritance mis-orders punctuation, instead of the natural left/start alignment LTR text needs. The same hardcoded TextAlign.right-on-translation pattern recurs in verse_card.dart (translation block uses TextAlign.justify with forced rtl at line 235-236).
impact: If a user picks an English (or other LTR) translation, the daily verse translation is forced flush-right with broken punctuation placement, looking misaligned and hard to read.
recommendation: Let translation text resolve its own direction: drop the explicit TextAlign.right (use TextAlign.start) and either omit textDirection or compute it from the translation's script, so LTR translations align left and RTL ones align right.
evidence:
Text(
  cleanTranslation,
  style: ...,
  textAlign: TextAlign.right,   // no textDirection; assumes RTL translation
  maxLines: 3,

verdict.reasoning:
The cited code is accurate. lib/features/home/widgets/daily_verse_card.dart lines 113-123 render the translation with textAlign: TextAlign.right and no textDirection, so it inherits the app-global RTL (app.dart wraps everything in Directionality(rtl)). lib/features/reader/widgets/verse_card.dart lines 235-236 use textAlign: TextAlign.justify with textDirection: TextDirection.rtl. Both hard-pin translation text to RTL with no per-script direction resolution, so an LTR (English/French) translation WOULD be misaligned and have mis-ordered punctuation. The widget-level pattern the claim describes is genuinely present.

However, the claim's premise that translations are user-selectable and can be non-Arabic does NOT hold in this codebase, which drops the real-world impact to near zero:
- The daily verse card fetches via getVerseByKey(verseKey) with no translationIds (lib/features/home/providers/daily_verse_provider.dart:28); quran_repository.dart:69-71 defaults that to const [16].
- Translation id 16 is التفسير الميسر / Al-Muyassar, which is Arabic/RTL (quran_constants.dart:158, translationOptions[0] language:'ar'; AL_MUYASSAR:16).
- There is NO translation-picker UI anywhere. translationOptions (which contains the LTR entries: Sahih International 131/en, Pickthall 20/en, Yusuf Ali 22/en, Hamidullah 136/fr) and setActiveTranslationIds are defined but referenced by no screen (grep finds them only in constants, provider, and datasource). The settings Reading section only exposes a boolean show/hide toggle (reading_section.dart:163-169).
- activeTranslationIds is permanently the hardcoded default [16] (settings_provider.dart:45), so verse_card.dart also only ever receives Arabic translation 16 via reader_provider.dart:11.

Thus, as the app actually ships and is operated, the translation is always Arabic (RTL) and TextAlign.right + RTL renders correctly; no LTR string ever reaches these widgets, so there is no user-visible misrendering today. It is a real latent code-quality defect (the fix to TextAlign.start with per-script direction is correct future-proofing) but not a medium-severity active alignment bug — the claim overstates impact by assuming a translation picker that does not exist. Downgraded to low.

title: Search-result verse uses hardcoded font instead of user's Quran font; redundant TextAlign.right
description: Search result verse text hardcodes fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New' rather than reading settings.quranFont (as verse_card, daily_verse_card, tafsir_sheet, share_sheet all do). The block also redundantly sets both textDirection: TextDirection.rtl and textAlign: TextAlign.right; in RTL, right == start, so TextAlign.right is unnecessary (consistent with the many other TextAlign.right-on-Arabic cases across the app).
impact: A user who selects Amiri or Hafs Smart as their Quran font sees search results in a different typeface than everywhere else, breaking visual consistency of Quranic text.
recommendation: Use fontFamily: settings.quranFont for the Arabic verse text in search results; optionally drop the redundant TextAlign.right (TextAlign.start is direction-aware).
evidence:
style: const TextStyle(
  fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New',
  fontSize: 24,
...
textDirection: TextDirection.rtl,
textAlign: TextAlign.right,

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed at lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart:257-268. Line 260 hardcodes fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New' for the search-result Arabic verse text. The app's default Quran font is 'Hafs Smart' (settings_local_datasource.dart:16, settings_provider.dart:40), and a user can change it via settings. Every other Arabic-verse renderer reads settings.quranFont: verse_card.dart (48/73/101/126/142), daily_verse_card.dart:103, tafsir_sheet.dart:162, share_sheet.dart:52, mushaf_view.dart (447/462/476/518), memorization_screen.dart:281. So a user who selects any Quran font sees the search-result verse render in a different font than everywhere else — a real, observable consistency gap. The fix is reachable: _buildSearchSlivers is a method on HomeScreen's ConsumerState (HomeScreen extends ConsumerStatefulWidget, ref used at lines 44/76/105), so ref.read(settingsProvider).quranFont is accessible. Severity low is correct: it is cosmetic, only manifests when the user changes the font away from the hardcoded one, and search rows are truncated to 3 lines. The secondary claim — that textAlign: TextAlign.right is redundant given explicit textDirection: TextDirection.rtl — is technically true (start resolves to right in RTL) but is a harmless style nit, not a flaw with user impact, and it is a pervasive idiom across the app (9 occurrences in 6 files); it does not change the verdict and the recommendation correctly marks it optional.

title: Default Quran font 'Hafs Smart' has no bold asset, but is used with FontWeight in ayah markers
description: Hafs Smart is the default verse font (settings_local_datasource returns 'Hafs Smart', settings_provider default 'Hafs Smart') yet pubspec registers only a single weight (HafsSmart8.ttf, no 700 asset). The ayah-marker style in verse_card._buildAyahMarkerStyle applies fontWeight: FontWeight.w600 with fontFamily: settings.quranFont (line 48-53). With only a regular asset registered, Flutter synthesizes a faux-bold for the Arabic ayah number glyph, which renders the diacritic-rich Hafs glyphs poorly or inconsistently versus the Amiri/Scheherazade bolds.
impact: Users on the default font see synthetic faux-bold ayah markers that look different from the real bold glyphs other fonts ship, and Noto Naskh (also regular-only) has the same issue.
recommendation: Either ship a Hafs Smart bold weight, or stop applying fontWeight.w600/bold to text rendered in single-weight Quran fonts (drop the weight for ayah markers, or gate bold to fonts that have a 700 asset).
evidence:
fonts: - family: Hafs Smart fonts: - asset: assets/fonts/HafsSmart8.ttf   // no weight: 700
// verse_card.dart:48-53 fontFamily: settings.quranFont, fontWeight: FontWeight.w600

verdict.reasoning:
Every cited fact is verified in the code. pubspec.yaml lines 88-90 register 'Hafs Smart' with a single asset (assets/fonts/HafsSmart8.ttf) and NO weight:700 entry — confirmed both in pubspec and the assets/fonts/ directory listing (only HafsSmart8.ttf exists, no bold). 'Hafs Smart' is genuinely the default Quran font: settings_local_datasource.dart:16 returns 'Hafs Smart' and settings_provider.dart:40 defaults quranFont to 'Hafs Smart' (and madinah script mode at line 154-155 even force-sets it). verse_card.dart:46-53 _buildAyahMarkerStyle() applies fontFamily: settings.quranFont with fontWeight: FontWeight.w600. Because only a regular weight is registered, Flutter synthesizes faux-bold for the ayah-marker glyph. The marker (formatAyahMarker / arabic_utils.dart:14-20) is a real Arabic glyph sequence (U+06DD end-of-ayah + Arabic-Indic digit), so faux-bold does apply to a diacritic/decoration-rich Arabic glyph, unlike Amiri/Scheherazade which ship genuine 700 assets. So the described mechanism is real, not speculation.

However, the medium severity is overstated. The faux-bold affects ONLY the small ayah-marker glyph (rendered at fontSize * 0.62, line 49) — a decorative numeral. The actual verse body text (verse_card.dart:125-130) correctly uses NO fontWeight, so it is unaffected. The visual artifact is a subtly thicker, possibly slightly distorted single marker glyph — a cosmetic inconsistency, not a readability or functional problem, and many users won't notice it. This warrants low severity, not medium. The recommendation (drop the w600 weight for single-weight Quran fonts, or ship a bold) is reasonable.

title: Cairo (global default fontFamily) has no bold asset despite pervasive FontWeight.bold usage
description: Cairo is the app-wide default fontFamily (app_theme.dart lines 9, 57, 105, 180) and the declared UI font (QuranTypography.uiFont='Cairo'), but pubspec registers only Cairo-Regular.ttf with no 700/bold variant. The UI uses FontWeight.bold / w600 / w700 extensively on Cairo-rendered text (titles, headers, labels across home, stats, settings, etc.). Flutter then synthesizes faux-bold for all of those, which is lower quality than a real Cairo Bold and inconsistent across the app.
impact: Every bold UI label/title/heading in the app (Arabic) is faux-bolded, looking smeared or uneven compared to a true bold cut. Affects most screens.
recommendation: Add Cairo-Bold.ttf (weight 700) to the Cairo family in pubspec, or pull Cairo from google_fonts with proper weights.
evidence: - family: Cairo fonts: - asset: assets/fonts/Cairo-Regular.ttf   // only regular; app uses FontWeight.bold everywhere on Cairo

verdict.reasoning: Verified against source. pubspec.yaml lines 91-93 register the Cairo family with ONLY Cairo-Regular.ttf and no weight:700 asset — confirmed, and conspicuously inconsistent with the Amiri (78-79) and Scheherazade New (82-84) families that both declare explicit Bold variants. Cairo is the app-wide default: app_theme.dart sets fontFamily:'Cairo' on all four themes (lines 9, 57, 105, 180) and theme_constants.dart line 31 declares uiFont='Cairo'. Bold weights are used pervasively on Cairo-inheriting UI text: 64 occurrences of FontWeight.bold/w600/w700 across 26 files. Spot-checked home_screen.dart line 169 (FontWeight.bold on a Text with no fontFamily override → inherits Cairo) while only the actual verse-text Text widgets explicitly set an Arabic font (lines 260 Scheherazade New, 393 Amiri, which DO have bold assets). So the vast majority of bold UI text renders via Flutter faux-bold (synthetic bolding) rather than a real Cairo Bold. The claim is accurate in every cited detail including the line numbers. However 'high' overstates it: this is a cosmetic rendering-quality degradation (faux-bold looks slightly heavier/smeared, especially on Arabic), not a functional/layout/navigation defect, and it degrades gracefully. Medium is the appropriate severity for an app-wide-but-cosmetic typography quality issue.

title: Home search results hardcode 'Scheherazade New', ignoring the user's selected Quran font
description: Verse search results on Home render the Arabic verse text with a hardcoded fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New' (fontSize 24, height 1.9), while every authoritative verse surface (verse_card, mushaf_view, daily_verse_card, tafsir_sheet, share_sheet, memorization) uses settings.quranFont (default 'Hafs Smart'). A user who picks Hafs Smart or Amiri still sees search-result verses in Scheherazade New.
impact: Verses look like a different script in search results than in the reader, breaking the sense of a consistent mushaf and confusing users who deliberately chose a font.
recommendation: Replace the hardcoded 'Scheherazade New' with the watched settings.quranFont (and use a shared verse text size constant instead of magic 24/1.9).
evidence: Text(result.text, style: const TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New', fontSize: 24, height: 1.9), ...)

verdict.reasoning: Verified verbatim at home_screen.dart:257-263: the verse search result renders result.text with `const TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Scheherazade New', fontSize: 24, height: 1.9)`. Because the style is `const` with an explicit fontFamily, it cannot reflect the user's setting and is not overridden by any TextTheme. The RTL Directionality/forced 'ar' locale only affect direction/localization, not fontFamily, so nothing mitigates it. Cross-checked the comparison set: settings.quranFont defaults to 'Hafs Smart' (settings_provider.dart:40, settings_local_datasource.dart:16) and is selectable from ['Hafs Smart','Scheherazade New','Amiri','Noto Naskh Arabic'] (reading_section.dart:77). Every other verse surface honors settings.quranFont — verse_card.dart (lines 48,73,101,126,142), mushaf_view.dart (447,462,476,518), daily_verse_card.dart:103, tafsir_sheet.dart:162, share_sheet.dart:52, memorization_screen.dart:281, chapter_header.dart:55 — making the home search result the sole outlier. So the inconsistency genuinely exists and is user-visible by default (Hafs Smart everywhere except search). However, severity 'high' is overstated: impact is limited to one secondary surface, font-family only, with no broken layout or accessibility failure (Scheherazade New is a valid registered font). Medium is more proportionate.

title: Arabic verse/surah text hardcodes 'Amiri' in bookmarks, notes, stats, chapter tiles and mushaf headers, ignoring quranFont
description: Saved-verse and surah-name Arabic text is hardcoded to fontFamily: 'Amiri' in multiple secondary screens: bookmarks_screen.dart:160 (saved verse text), notes_screen.dart:102 (saved verse text), stats_screen.dart:164 (surah name), home_screen.dart:393 (_ChapterTile surah name), mushaf_view.dart:296/320/505 (surah/juz header + inline chapter name), chapter_header.dart:32 (reader chapter title), juz_navigator_screen.dart:54, mushaf_navigation_sheet.dart (multiple). None of these honor settings.quranFont, so a user who selects Hafs Smart or Scheherazade still sees Amiri for these strings.
impact: The chosen Quran font is silently overridden in many places, producing visibly different letterforms for the same verses/surah names across screens and inconsistent typography throughout the app.
recommendation: Decide a single rule: either always use settings.quranFont for Arabic verse text and a single dedicated decorative font constant for surah-name headers, then apply it uniformly. Centralize in a constant rather than re-typing 'Amiri'.
evidence: bookmarks_screen.dart: Text(bookmark.text, style: const TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Amiri', fontSize: 16, height: 1.8), ...)  // notes_screen, stats_screen, home _ChapterTile, mushaf_view all do the same

title: No fontFamilyFallback anywhere; non-registered or missing glyphs fall back to platform default with no Arabic chain
description: A grep of the entire lib/ tree for 'fontFamilyFallback' returns zero matches. No TextStyle and none of the ThemeData definitions provide an Arabic fallback chain. The pubspec registers single-weight families (Hafs Smart, Noto Naskh, Cairo) with no fallback. If any Quran font lacks a particular glyph (e.g., certain tajweed/pause marks or rare diacritics) or a font fails to load, text silently renders in the OS default font with no Arabic-aware fallback, risking tofu boxes or mismatched glyphs.
impact: Rare-but-real glyph gaps (especially in single-weight fonts like Hafs Smart / Noto Naskh) can show missing-glyph boxes or jarring fallback fonts mid-verse, with no controlled fallback.
recommendation: Add fontFamilyFallback (e.g., ['Amiri','Scheherazade New','Noto Naskh Arabic']) to verse TextStyles, and a Cairo->Noto Naskh UI fallback in ThemeData, so missing glyphs degrade gracefully within the Arabic font family set.
evidence: grep 'fontFamilyFallback' lib/  -> No matches found

verdict.reasoning: The factual basis of the claim is fully verified. Grep for `fontFamilyFallback` across the entire lib/ tree returns zero matches. lib/core/theme/app_theme.dart sets a bare `fontFamily: 'Cairo'` at lines 9, 57, 105, and 180 with no fallback chain. pubspec.yaml registers single-asset families (Noto Naskh Arabic, Hafs Smart, Cairo) and no family declares a fallback. Every verse-rendering TextStyle uses a bare `fontFamily` with no fallback: verse_card.dart (lines 48/73/101/126/142), mushaf_view.dart, tajweed_text.dart, reader_screen.dart line 350 ('Amiri'), etc. So the described gap genuinely exists.\n\nHowever, the SEVERITY is overstated. This is a defensive/hardening gap, not an active defect: (1) The Arabic fonts actually in use — Amiri, Scheherazade New, Hafs Smart — are full-coverage Uthmani fonts with complete diacritic and pause-mark support, so the bundled Quran text renders correctly in practice; there is no observed tofu. (2) The claim's premise that missing glyphs would render 'with no Arabic-aware fallback' is partly wrong — when Flutter has no fontFamilyFallback it falls through to the platform default, and most target OSes (Android/iOS) ship Arabic-capable system fonts, so Arabic glyphs typically still render. The real risk is narrow: a font asset failing to load or an extremely rare glyph outside the chosen font. Probability of user-visible failure is low. It is a legitimate best-practice improvement (adding a fallback chain is cheap and correct), but it is a low-severity robustness nit, not a medium-impact UX flaw.

title: App-wide accent ignores theme tokens (~66 hardcoded Color(0xFFD97706))
description: theme_constants.dart defines three distinct accent tokens (appAccentColor #D97706 for light/dark, appAccentColorLight #F59E0B, appAccentColorAmoled #FFB74D) and app_theme.dart wires them into each ColorScheme.primary. impact: Accent color is inconsistent between the player and the rest of the app in AMOLED, and changing the brand color later requires editing 21 files. AMOLED/sepia never get their intended accent on these controls.
recommendation: Replace const Color(0xFFD97706) with Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary (or a single Theme extension token). Per-theme primary is already correctly defined in app_theme.dart, so this alone fixes AMOLED/sepia parity.
evidence: activeTrackColor: const Color(0xFFD97706), ... thumbColor: const Color(0xFFD97706), ... foregroundColor: const Color(0xFFD97706),

verdict.reasoning: Verified against source. theme_constants.dart lines 122-124 define three distinct accent tokens: appAccentColor #D97706, appAccentColorLight #F59E0B, appAccentColorAmoled #FFB74D. app_theme.dart wires them per-theme: amoled() sets colorScheme.primary = appAccentColorAmoled (#FFB74D, line 186) and bottom nav selectedItemColor = appAccentColorAmoled (line 211); sepia() uses #D97706 primary. audio_player_bar.dart hardcodes const Color(0xFFD97706) at every cited line (40,42,43 slider; 128 loading spinner; 142,143 play button; 167,173 speed menu; 217,223,235,245,255 repeat chip/menu) — 13 occurrences, the most of any file. The RTL/Directionality wrapper has no bearing on color and does not mitigate this; there is no default fallback. The claim's evidence strings and line numbers are accurate (it even undercounts the file's occurrences). Downgrading severity from high to medium: the defect is real and architecture-violating but is a cosmetic two-shade amber mismatch, not a functional/contrast/accessibility break — high overstates a single-color polish issue.

title: Color(0xFFD97706) accent is amber-on-cream in sepia theme (low contrast)
description: The sepia theme background is SepiaColors.background #FFFBEB (pale cream) and primary is set to #D97706. Small accent labels like Colors.amber[700] (#FFA000) are even lighter and fail harder.
impact: Accent labels and small text are hard to read in sepia mode, which is the mode users pick specifically for comfortable reading.
recommendation: Darken the sepia accent (e.g. use SepiaColors.textMuted #92400E for accent text) or route accent text through a higher-contrast theme token rather than the bright #D97706/amber[700].
evidence: static const Color background = Color(0xFFFFFBEB); ... primary: const Color(0xFFD97706),

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed against source. lib/core/theme/app_theme.dart sepia() (lines 106-117) sets seedColor and primary to const Color(0xFFD97706), surface and scaffoldBackgroundColor to SepiaColors.background, and theme_constants.dart line 80 defines SepiaColors.background = Color(0xFFFFFBEB) (pale cream). Severity stays high: amber[700] dropping to ~2:1 is a severe, demonstrable text-contrast failure; it is only mitigated slightly by affecting one opt-in theme and some targets being non-text UI controls (which only need 3:1, where D97706 sits right at the edge).

title: AMOLED cards use #D97706 tints/fills instead of the brighter AMOLED accent
description: The mini audio player (shown on every shell screen) hardcodes Color(0xFFD97706) for its progress bar, music-note icon, and play/pause icon. theme_constants.dart deliberately defines appAccentColorAmoled #FFB74D ('avoid #D97706 on pure black') and app_theme.dart sets it as the AMOLED primary. The persistent player ignores that and shows the darker #D97706 on #000000, contradicting the design intent stated in the AMOLED color comments.

recommendation: Use theme.colorScheme.primary in app_shell mini player so AMOLED gets #FFB74D and sepia gets its accent automatically.
evidence: valueColor: const AlwaysStoppedAnimation(Color(0xFFD97706)), ... color: Color(0xFFD97706), // music_note

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed in code. lib/core/widgets/app_shell.dart hardcodes Color(0xFFD97706) at the cited lines: 93 (progress bar valueColor), 106 (music_note icon), 135 (loading CircularProgressIndicator), and 140 (play/pause icon). The _MiniAudioPlayer already receives `theme` and uses theme.colorScheme.surface (line 81) and onSurface (lines 119, 156), so it could trivially use theme.colorScheme.primary instead. The design intent is real: theme_constants.dart:124 defines appAccentColorAmoled = #FFB74D, and app_theme.dart sets the AMOLED ColorScheme primary to appAccentColorAmoled (line 186) over a pure-black #000000 surface (lines 184, 192), with every other primary-accented element (nav selectedItemColor line 211, input focusedBorder line 227) using the brighter #FFB74D. verdict.reasoning: All cited lines are accurate. lib/features/home/screens/home_screen.dart uses raw material greens for the 'completed chapter' state: line 351 valueColor Colors.green, line 360 Colors.green.withValues(alpha:0.1) container bg, line 374 Colors.green[700] chapter-number text, lines 452/458 Colors.green[600] for the check_circle icon and 'مكتملة' text. The pattern repeats in stats_screen.dart (190,201), khatmah_screen.dart (300,316,358,362,367), and memorization_screen.dart (324,332), confirming the systemic nature. The contrast concern is real: AmoledColors.background is #000000 and surface #0A0A0A (confirmed in theme_constants.dart). recommendation: Use selectedColor: theme.colorScheme.primary and labelStyle color: theme.colorScheme.onPrimary so the foreground/background pair always matches the active theme.
evidence: selectedColor: const Color(0xFFD97706), labelStyle: TextStyle(color: selected ? Colors.white : null,

verdict.reasoning: Code confirmed exactly. tafsir_sheet.dart:111-113 sets selectedColor: const Color(0xFFD97706) with labelStyle color: selected ? Colors.white : null, bypassing ColorScheme.primary/onPrimary. khatmah_screen.dart:47-49 (ChoiceChip) does the same. title: Memorization verse-range TextFields recreate their controller every build, breaking input

Their onChanged handlers (lines 101-104, 113-116) call setState whenever int.tryParse succeeds and n>0, which triggers a rebuild that recreates the controller with the new value. description: Once the learner reveals every word with 'كشف الكل' (sets _showAll=true), the only control is a toggle that flips back to 'إخفاء' showing the SAME hidden indices again. There is no 'new round' / re-randomize action. _hideRandomWords() is only ever called once, from a postFrame callback gated on `_hiddenWordIndices.isEmpty && index == 0`, so after the first round the set is frozen for the whole session. To practice a fresh set of blanks the user must tap 'رجوع' to exit, then 'بدء المراجعة' again.
impact: The core practice loop is one-shot. After revealing the answers there is no forward action to continue practicing the same passage, which is exactly what a memorization tool should support. Users hit a dead end and must back out and restart.
recommendation: Add a 'جولة جديدة' (new round) button that calls _hideRandomWords(words) again (resetting _score/_total/_showAll), and drive auto-hide from _startMemorization rather than a one-time build-phase callback.

verdict.reasoning: Verified against the code. The controls bar (lines 165-178) contains only 'رجوع' (back) and a single FilledButton.tonal that toggles _showAll between 'كشف الكل' and 'إخفاء'. When _showAll is flipped back to false, line 257 (`_hiddenWordIndices.contains(wi) && !_showAll`) re-hides the EXACT SAME indices — the set is never re-randomized. _hideRandomWords() is defined at line 37 and, per grep, called only once at line 196, inside a postFrame callback gated on `_hiddenWordIndices.isEmpty && index == 0` (lines 193-198). There is no 'new round'/re-randomize button anywhere, so the cited dead-end is accurate: after 'كشف الكل', the user can only re-show the same blanks. The workaround is to tap رجوع then بدء المراجعة again. One nuance the claim overstates: the set is not strictly 'frozen for the whole session' — if the user reveals every hidden word by tapping (line 262 shrinks _hiddenWordIndices), it can become empty and the line-193 gate re-fires, generating a fresh random set on the next rebuild (and that path is itself buggy: _score is never reset, only _total at line 44). But that side effect does not rescue the _showAll path the claim targets, so the flaw stands. Severity lowered from high to medium: this is a non-primary feature reachable only via the Home AppBar overflow menu, with a trivial 2-tap workaround and no data loss or hard block, though it does undermine the core repeat-practice loop of a memorization tool.

title: Tab switch to Bookmarks/Settings and back loses selected-category filter and scroll
description: _selectedCategory lives in widget State and the shell tabs use go()+NoTransitionPage. Because the bottom-nav destinations are rebuilt rather than kept alive, leaving the Bookmarks tab and returning resets _selectedCategory back to 'all' and discards the ListView scroll offset. The same applies to any in-screen filter state on tab screens.
impact: A user who filters to e.g. 'حفظ' bookmarks, taps another tab, and returns is silently dumped back to the unfiltered top of the list, losing their place and filter context.
recommendation: Persist _selectedCategory in a provider (or use AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin / IndexedStack in the shell) so filter and scroll survive tab switches.
evidence: class _BookmarksScreenState ... { String _selectedCategory = 'all'; ... }  // ephemeral State, no keep-alive

verdict.reasoning:
The claim is technically accurate and code-grounded. Confirmed: bookmarks_screen.dart:18 declares String _selectedCategory = all as ephemeral widget State in _BookmarksScreenState (a ConsumerState), and the ListView (lines 78-175) has no PageStorageKey or restorationId. app_shell.dart:36-44 switches tabs via context.goNamed(). app_router.dart:23-49 uses a plain ShellRoute whose three child GoRoutes each render via NoTransitionPage. A plain GoRouter ShellRoute (unlike StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack) does NOT keep inactive branch state alive; the inactive route element is disposed when navigating away, so Bookmarks to Settings to Bookmarks re-runs createState() and resets _selectedCategory to all and discards the scroll offset. A repo-wide grep for AutomaticKeepAlive, StatefulShellRoute, IndexedStack, restorationId, PageStorageKey returned no matches, confirming nothing mitigates this. The bookmark data itself survives via the Riverpod bookmarkProvider, so this is a UI-state reset (filter plus scroll), not data loss. The recommendation (provider-backed filter, AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin, or StatefulShellRoute) is correct. I downgrade severity from medium to low: impact is a minor transient inconvenience (filter snaps back to all, list scrolls to top) for users who filter by category then tab away and return; no data loss, no broken flow, and bookmark lists are typically short.</parameter>
